title: fix(vgi-bridge): post the check only against the protected base
body:
fix(vgi-bridge): post the check only against the protected base

Addresses the PR #67 review.

HIGH — check-run carry-over: a check run attaches to a commit, so the
bridge now posts only when the base is the repository's default branch
(what the managed ruleset protects), read from GitHub at check time; for
any other base it posts nothing. A pull request's base and head are
re-read from GitHub, a base edit is checked against the new base,
de-duplication and `external_id` are keyed by (repo, head, base branch),
and an empty range is a success only when the head is the base tip.

- The bridge-posted check is gated on the installation's permissions and
  event subscriptions, recorded at bind, restored, and re-probed when an
  installation accepts new permissions (the documented upgrade path).
- `check_run` / `check_suite` rerequests re-run the check; a delivery is
  recorded as handled only after its checks posted, so a redelivery after
  a failed post runs again.
- A job's result and its outbox entry are written in one transaction; a
  repeat of a finished job always re-sends the result rebuilt from the
  ledger, even after an acknowledgement.
- The fetch is a partial clone of commit objects only (`tree:0`, falling
  back to `blob:none`) with a byte bound; commits are read with the same
  hardened git (cleared env, no lazy fetch).
- Inbound proofs must be `assertionMethod`.
- `app_owner` is required (with `app_owner_is_user`); a failed manifest
  exchange leaves the registration link usable; `platform_keyring_file` is
  optional.
- The master key's environment variable is cleared once read (from the
  single-threaded `main`); the registry endpoint is rediscovered after a
  registry failure.
- Tests for each, a falsifiable fetch test (no trees, bare), and one test
  through the real VerifyTrustVerifier (did:key-signed commits, a local
  registry stub, the namespace fallback).

title: fix(vgi-forge-github): what the bridge-posted check needs to be safe
body:
fix(vgi-forge-github): what the bridge-posted check needs to be safe

Addresses the PR #67 review (adapter side).

- Check triggers carry the base branch, and the adapter can read the
  repository's default branch and a pull request's current head and base,
  so the bridge can post only against the protected base (a check run
  attaches to a commit: a success against any other base would count for
  the protected one too).
- Base edits (`pull_request` `edited` with `changes.base`) and this App's
  `check_run` / `check_suite` `rerequested` are triggers; the manifest
  subscribes to `check_run` and `check_suite`.
- The comparison is read across pages (100 per page, 250 in all), so a
  range of 101-250 commits is no longer reported truncated.
- The manifest adds Pull requests and Merge queues (read), which GitHub
  requires for the `pull_request` and `merge_group` events.
- `bridge_posted_check` now also needs the installation to hold checks
  write, pull requests and merge queues read, and both event
  subscriptions (`set_bridge_checks_ready`, `detect_bridge_checks`, set at
  bind); without them the namespace keeps the Actions workflow and the
  bind reports what is missing, events included.
- The bridge-posted plan no longer needs a platform keyring.

title: feat(vtc): a console signing key is a credential of the operator's admin DID
body:
Server side of #1684, against the design note merged in #1685
(`docs/05-design-notes/vtc-console-signing.md`, Option A). Unblocks the bearer
routes #1641 would retire — 34 of the 49 are console-reachable, including all
four #1681 kept — by giving the admin console a key it can sign with.

**A console signing key is a credential of the operator's existing admin DID,
the way a passkey is.** Not an identity of its own, and not an ACL row: giving
a console key its own admin row is self-promotion by a longer path and #1658's
`Invariant::SelfPromotion` (VTI-OPS-050) refuses it. What the VTC stores is a
*delegation* — "console key K may act as admin DID D" — which confers no role.
Authority remains D's ACL row, read at execution time, so the property #1681
established (`admin_signer` never consults `sessions_ks`) survives intact.

## What is here

- **`console_keys` keyspace** — `console_key:<consoleDid>` → the delegation.
  `EXCLUDED_FROM_BACKUP`, and that one is a security decision rather than
  housekeeping: a restore into a rebuilt host, a staging clone or different
  hands must not hand a browser profile the ability to sign as an administrator
  again. Recorded in `keyspaces.rs` and `docs/03-vtc/backup-restore.md`.
- **Enrolment behind the step-up the console already runs.** `AdminAuth` plus
  `acl::elevation::verified`, which reads the **session row** — a stolen
  session alone cannot leave a signing key behind. The subject is the proven
  caller and the body cannot name it, so self-targeted is the only case this
  surface can express. That inverts `acl/grant`'s rule deliberately, and the
  code says why: a delegation confers nothing, so there is nothing to promote,
  and it is a credential of *your* identity.
- **Verification.** `admin_signer` gains one step: a signer with **no ACL row
  of its own** may be a delegated console key, in which case the delegating
  admin's row is resolved — at execution time, as before. A signer that *has*
  a row is answered by that row, including when it refuses; the design note
  sketches falling through on `Forbidden` too, and this is deliberately tighter
  so a stale delegation cannot route around a demotion.
- **List and revoke**, modelled on the passkey management surface. Revocation
  tombstones the row (a burned key cannot be re-enrolled), takes effect on the
  very next document, and needs no second factor — an operator who suspects a
  browser should not have to find their authenticator before disowning it.
- **Audit.** `AdminConsoleKeyEnrolled` / `AdminConsoleKeyRevoked` on
  `vti_common::audit::AuditEvent` (which is `#[non_exhaustive]`, so additive),
  actor = the human, target = the console DID.

## No published Trust Task covers this

Checked `trust_tasks_rs::schema_index` and both candidate families.
`device/register/0.1` registers a device as a consumer in its own right, with
`consumerKind`, an HPKE recipient key and a granted `Capability` set — an
identity with its own authority, which is the shape VTI-OPS-050 refuses here.
`auth/passkey/{enroll,revoke,list}` is WebAuthn end to end and describes
nothing about a `did:key` a browser minted for itself.

So per the workspace rule (a new family needs an upstream specification first)
these are served on the existing REST surface, mounted **without** a Trust-Task
binding — the same exemption `relationships::{suspend,restore}` and the
`schemas` routes carry, and for the same reason: binding an invented
`trusttasks.org/spec/…` URI asserts the registry serves it, which
`trust_task_manifest.rs` checks, and raising that test's exception count is
explicitly the wrong fix.

`routes/admin/console_keys.rs` records what the upstream task should be: an
`auth/signing-key/{enroll,list,revoke}` family, sibling to `auth/passkey/*`,
with `enroll` taking `{ signingKeyDid, deviceLabel?, expiresAt? }` and **no**
subject member. The bodies below are already those payloads.

## The wire format the console PR implements against

```
POST /v1/admin/console-keys        AdminAuth + live step-up
  → { "consoleDid": "did:key:z6Mk…", "label": "Work laptop", "expiresAt": "…"? }
  ← 201 ConsoleKey
  ← 403 { "error": "step_up_required" }   run the passkey step-up, retry
  ← 409                                   already enrolled / holds an ACL row
  ← 400                                   not a did:key, or the caller's own DID

GET  /v1/admin/console-keys        AdminAuth
  ← 200 { "consoleKeys": [ ConsoleKey, … ] }   the caller's own, newest first,
                                               revoked ones included

DELETE /v1/admin/console-keys/{consoleDid}     AdminAuth, self or super-admin
  ← 200 { "consoleDid", "revokedAt", "remainingActive" }

ConsoleKey = {
  consoleDid, adminDid, label?, createdAt,
  expiresAt?, lastUsedAt?, revokedAt?, active
}
```

`active` is computed server-side on purpose — the console must not
re-implement the predicate the verifier uses, because the two disagreeing is
how a page shows a key as working after it stopped.

`openapi.json` + `src/lib/wire.ts` are regenerated; `npm run lint` passes.

## What the console PR must still do

Generate the key with `crypto.subtle.generateKey({name:"Ed25519"}, **false**,
["sign","verify"])` and assert `privateKey.extractable === false` — §4b of the
note measures that `true` costs nothing and exposes the private key to any
script in the origin (the did-hosting-ui defect). Store the `CryptoKey` objects
in IndexedDB, never bytes. Derive `did:key:z6Mk…`, POST it here behind
`stepUpSession()`, and sign at the one `src/lib/api.ts` seam with `created`
back-dated 60 s. Then move `plugins/members.tsx` onto `POST /v1/trust-tasks` —
checking `members/update`'s `extensions` bag against the signed door's 64 KiB
cap first — and add the key list beside `myPasskeys.tsx`.

## Security properties, each with a test

| property | where |
|---|---|
| cannot enrol without a fresh step-up, and nothing is written | `tests/admin_console_keys.rs::enrolment_without_a_fresh_step_up_is_refused` |
| cannot enrol for another DID (no subject member; `deny_unknown_fields`) | `a_body_naming_another_admin_does_not_parse` |
| cannot delegate to a DID that holds an ACL row (a demotion that would silently promote) | `a_did_that_already_holds_an_acl_row_cannot_be_enrolled` |
| a second admin cannot claim an enrolled key | `a_second_admin_cannot_claim_an_enrolled_console_key` |
| a console key gains **no bearer authority**, so it cannot enrol further delegations or escalate | `a_console_key_gains_no_bearer_authority` |
| revocation stops authorization on the next document | `trust_tasks::…::a_revoked_delegation_stops_authorizing_immediately` |
| the admin's row removed / demoted / expired stops it | `removing_the_admins_acl_row_…`, `demoting_the_admin_…`, `an_expired_admin_row_…` |
| a delegation inherits its admin's ceiling and no more | `a_delegation_inherits_its_admins_ceiling_and_no_more` |
| a signer with its own row is never answered by a delegation | `a_signer_holding_its_own_row_is_never_answered_by_a_delegation` |
| enrolment and revocation are audited | `enrolment_and_revocation_are_both_audited` |

Closes nothing on its own — #1684 stays open for the console client.

Refs #1684, #1641.

title: feat(vtc): a console signing key is a credential of the operator's admin DID (#1692)
body:
feat(vtc): a console signing key is a credential of the operator's admin DID (#1692)

Server side of #1684, against the design note merged in #1685
(`vtc-console-signing.md`, Option A). The admin console cannot author a signed
Trust Task document, which is what keeps every bearer route #1641 would retire
mounted — 34 of the 49 are console-reachable, including all four #1681 kept.

A console signing key is a credential of the operator's existing admin DID, the
way a passkey is. Not an identity of its own and not an ACL row: giving a
console key its own admin row is self-promotion by a longer path, and #1658's
`Invariant::SelfPromotion` (VTI-OPS-050) refuses it. What the VTC stores is a
delegation — "console key K may act as admin DID D" — which confers no role.
Authority remains D's ACL row, read at execution time, so the property #1681
established (`admin_signer` never consults `sessions_ks`) survives intact.

- `console_keys` keyspace, `console_key:<consoleDid>` → the delegation, and
  EXCLUDED_FROM_BACKUP. That exclusion is a security decision rather than
  housekeeping: a restore into a rebuilt host, a staging clone or different
  hands must not hand a browser profile the ability to sign as an administrator
  again.
- Enrolment behind `AdminAuth` plus `acl::elevation::verified`, which reads the
  session row — a stolen session alone cannot leave a signing key behind. The
  subject is the proven caller and the body cannot name it, so self-targeted is
  the only case this surface can express. That inverts `acl/grant`'s rule
  deliberately: a delegation confers nothing, so there is nothing to promote,
  and it is a credential of your own identity.
- `admin_signer` gains one step. A signer with no ACL row of its own may be a
  delegated console key, in which case the delegating admin's row is resolved,
  at execution time, as before. A signer that has a row is answered by that row,
  including when it refuses — tighter than the note's sketch, so a stale
  delegation cannot route around a demotion.
- List and revoke on the passkey management model. Revocation tombstones the row
  (a burned key cannot be re-enrolled), takes effect on the next document, and
  needs no second factor: an operator who suspects a browser should not have to
  find their authenticator before disowning it.
- `AdminConsoleKeyEnrolled` / `AdminConsoleKeyRevoked` audit events.

No published Trust Task covers this. `device/register/0.1` registers a device as
a consumer in its own right, with a granted `Capability` set — the shape
VTI-OPS-050 refuses here — and `auth/passkey/*` is WebAuthn end to end. So the
three routes are mounted without a Trust-Task binding, the same exemption
`relationships::{suspend,restore}` carries, and `routes/admin/console_keys.rs`
records what the upstream `auth/signing-key/{enroll,list,revoke}` family should
be. The bodies here are already those payloads.

Refs #1684, #1641.

title: fix(vtc)!: the registry syncer publishes only members who consented
body:
## Keyring round 3, Q14 follow-up: the syncer publishes members who declined

Keyring (Berkman Center's Keyring wallet team) asked what `registryConsent` on `vtc/join-requests/submit` does (round-3 **Q14**; it has no VTI-nn number). #1682 carried the answer onto `Member::publish_consent` and said plainly that nothing enforced it. This PR is the enforcement it deferred.

> ### ⚠️ Behaviour change: only members who consented are published
> After this PR, the default deployment publishes **only members whose `publishConsent` is `true`**. Before, it published every new member.
> **Existing deployments:** every member admitted before #1682 holds `publishConsent = false`, and may already be in the registry. Their record is **removed** the next time the syncer re-decides that member: a role change, a consent change, a retried job, or an audit-log replay. Nothing removes them all at once on upgrade. This is the intended result, since they never consented. To keep a member listed **who agrees to it**:
> ```bash
> curl -X PATCH "$VTC/v1/members/$MEMBER_DID" \
>   -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
>   -d '{"publishConsent": true}'
> ```
> (or the `vtc/members/update` Trust Task). The same text is in `docs/03-vtc/trust-registry.md` → *Who is published: member consent*.

### Root cause

Per submit 0.2 (*Consent/purpose* section, and the payload schema), `registryConsent` is the applicant's consent to trust-registry publication. `registry/tail.rs` turned every `MemberAdded` into a `PublishMember` job. `syncer.rs` then gated that job only on `registry.rego`'s `publish_on_join` (default `true`), evaluated with an empty input. Neither file read `publish_consent`. There were also two side doors:
- `RoleChanged` → `UpdateMember` published an `Active` record with no gate at all.
- `MarkDeparted` published a `Departed` record for members who had never been published. That disclosed the membership at the moment it ended.

### What changed

`MembershipSyncer::resolve` decides each job **at dispatch time from current state**. The same logic covers retries, `vtc sync-jobs retry`, and replays.

| job | member | we published it (mirror row) | action |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DeleteMember` | any | any | delete |
| `MarkDeparted` | any | yes / no | publish `Departed` / **skip** |
| `Publish`/`UpdateMember` | missing or removed | any | skip (the removal job owns the record) |
| `Publish`/`UpdateMember` | live, no consent | yes / no | **withdraw (delete)** / skip |
| `PublishMember`, or `UpdateMember` on first publication | live, consented | — | `publish_on_join` → publish / skip |
| `UpdateMember` | live, consented | yes | publish |

- **Consent is a hard floor, enforced in code. No policy can publish a member who did not consent**, because consent is the applicant's to give and not the community's. `publish_on_join` can only narrow. It now receives `{action: "publish", member: {did, publishConsent}}`, which matches the input shape the rego header already documented.
- **Withdrawal:** a `MemberUpdated` whose `fields_changed` includes `publishConsent` now enqueues an `UpdateMember`. `true→false` deletes the registry record and the mirror row. It is a delete, not `Departed`, because the member has not left. `false→true` publishes, subject to the policy.
- `MembershipSyncer::new` now requires the members keyspace, and `evaluate_publish_on_join` now takes the input. `vtc-service` is `publish = false`, so neither is a public API break.
- Doc updates: the `Member::publish_consent` doc comment, the `registry.rego` output-contract comment, and the registry/syncer/tail module docs. `docs/03-vtc/trust-registry.md` gets a new section, and the `community-lifecycle.md` policy table is updated.

**Known limit:** "we published it" means the local `registry_records` mirror row. If a mirror write failed after a successful publish (logged as a warning), a later withdrawal or departure for that member skips. Drift detection surfaces such a member as `unknownLocally`.

### Tests

New tests in `registry::syncer`:
- `a_member_who_did_not_consent_is_not_published_on_join` (with `publish_on_join := true`)
- `a_policy_reading_publish_consent_sees_it_in_the_input`
- `withdrawing_consent_removes_the_record`
- `granting_consent_later_publishes_the_member`
- `a_late_grant_still_answers_to_publish_on_join`
- `a_role_change_does_not_publish_a_member_who_did_not_consent`
- `a_departure_of_a_never_published_member_publishes_nothing`
- `a_replay_honours_current_consent` (cursor reset: the legacy non-consenting record is removed, the consenting member stays)

Also new: `registry::tail::member_updated_enqueues_only_for_a_publish_consent_change`. The existing syncer tests now seed a consenting member.

Run:
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --no-fail-fast` (default features, incl. `tsp`): all green
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo fmt --all`
- `cargo doc -D warnings`: no new errors. The failures that remain are all in files this PR does not touch, and `main` shows them too.

### Checklist
- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): n/a
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): no locks added
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1): the mirror row is still written or deleted only after the registry call succeeds
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off (R1.4): a local read failure in `resolve` goes through `record_failure` (the job's backoff and max attempts), and registry health is left alone
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): unchanged
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): a skipped job is deleted before its outcome is audited, as before
- [x] New/changed wire types (R3.*): no wire change. The policy input is new, uses camelCase `publishConsent`, and matches the member wire form
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*): a missing or removed member row, or absent consent, means not published. A broken policy still skips
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.*): withdrawals log at info, skips at debug with the reason
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" (R2.1): decisions are re-derived on every dispatch, so a crash before the mirror update re-decides from current state
- [x] Deviations flagged: the default-behaviour change above, which was approved

title: fix(vtc)!: the registry syncer publishes only members who consented (#1691)
body:
fix(vtc)!: the registry syncer publishes only members who consented (#1691)

`registryConsent` on `vtc/join-requests/submit` is the applicant's consent
to trust-registry publication (submit 0.2, Consent/purpose). #1682 carried
it onto `Member::publish_consent`, but the MembershipSyncer never read the
flag. It published every `MemberAdded` when `registry.rego`'s
`publish_on_join` was true (the default), so members who declined were
listed in the community's trust-registry record anyway.

The syncer now decides each job at dispatch time from current state:

- Consent is a hard floor enforced in code. A live member is published
  only while `publish_consent` is true. No policy can publish a member
  who did not consent, because consent is the applicant's to give and
  not the community's.
- `publish_on_join` narrows. It is consulted only for a consenting
  member, on first publication, whichever job asks (`PublishMember`, or
  an `UpdateMember` for a member not yet published). A late grant or a
  role change no longer routes around `publish_on_join := false`. The
  rule's input is now `{action: "publish", member: {did, publishConsent}}`.
- Withdrawal: a `MemberUpdated` that changes `publishConsent` enqueues
  an `UpdateMember`. Withdrawn (true -> false) deletes the member's
  registry record and mirror row. Granted (false -> true) publishes,
  subject to the policy.
- A `MarkDeparted` for a member who was never published is skipped.
  Otherwise it would publish a `Departed` record and disclose the
  membership as it ends.

BEHAVIOUR CHANGE: every member admitted before #1682 holds
`publishConsent = false`. Such a member may already be in the registry.
Their record is removed the next time the syncer re-decides them: a role
change, a consent change, a retried job, or an audit-log replay. Nothing
removes them all at once on upgrade. To keep a member listed who agrees
to it, set `{"publishConsent": true}` via `PATCH /v1/members/{did}` or
`vtc/members/update` (see docs/03-vtc/trust-registry.md, "Who is
published: member consent").

`MembershipSyncer::new` takes the members keyspace, and
`evaluate_publish_on_join` takes the policy input. vtc-service is
`publish = false`.

title: feat(persona)!: worlds on the wire, and a narrow read of one attribute
body:
Takes **trust-tasks-rs 0.22**, unreachable since 0.21.21: `affinidi-messaging-sdk` required `^0.21.20`, and `MediatorAcl` crosses that SDK's API, so a graph holding both versions failed to compile rather than carrying a tolerable duplicate. affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#885 moved the messaging crates; this takes the line they are now on. The lockfile moves only the twelve crates this needs — one `trust-tasks-rs`, one `affinidi-messaging-sdk`, one `affinidi-tdk`.

### Worlds (spec dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#610)

`persona/facet/*` → `persona/world/*`, `facetId` → `worldId`, and `correlation/analyze` takes a **1.1** for its three renamed members. `face` and `facet` shared a stem while naming different things — a projection of the pool, and an arrangement of those projections — and every UI had already resolved it by saying "world", which left the collision live for anyone reading both.

**The retired spellings stay routable for one release and answer in their own words**: `facetId` for `worldId`, `facets` for `worlds`, `crossesFacets` for `crossesWorlds`. A document already issued against a retired specification still validates, and refusing it would break a caller for a rename that costs it nothing. The aliases are written out rather than threaded through the live handlers as a parameter, so the whole thing is one `git rm` when the window closes — handlers, three `REACH` rows, three dispatch arms, three SDK constants.

The `pf:` storage prefix is **unchanged**: an opaque key prefix, not the noun. Renaming it would orphan every world already stored.

### `persona/attribute/get` (spec dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#616)

Reading one value meant `attribute/list` with a type prefix, filtered client-side — so revealing one email address decrypted **every** email address the holder has, and the audit row recorded a listing of the pool rather than a decision about one fact.

`PersonaStore::get_attribute` applies exactly what a listing applies — visibility, retention, credential re-derivation — because a read that answered differently depending on which task asked would be a second set of rules to keep in step. `versionPurged` is distinct from `notFound` (the attribute is there; that version is not), and `retainedVersions` lets a holder see what purging would take away instead of deciding blind.

### Two latent defects, found by the new tests

- **`correlation/analyze/1.0` was already answering with 1.1's member names.** The handler emitted `crossesWorlds`/`worldIds`; nothing noticed because 1.1 did not exist yet. Now 1.1 is dispatched and 1.0 is answered in its own words.
- **An empty world failed its own response schema.** `faceIds` and `attributeIds` carried `skip_serializing_if = "Vec::is_empty"` while the schema requires them, so listing a world with no members returned a 500 `responseSchemaViolation`. It predates the rename; no test had ever made an empty one. The world/list conformance witness now uses exactly that shape.

### Tests

`one_attribute_is_read_by_name_and_says_what_it_withheld` (default withholding, the second flag for sensitive, `notFound` vs `versionPurged`) and `a_world_answers_to_its_retired_name_in_that_names_words` (one store, two spellings, each response in the words of the task sent). Plus the four registries the workspace keeps — retry-safety classification, reach, dispatch, and conformance witnesses — each of which caught a gap.

CI set run locally: fmt, clippy `-D warnings`, workspace (4840), vtc (1883).

title: feat(vgi-bridge): the per-community bridge service
body:
feat(vgi-bridge): the per-community bridge service

The service design §5.7 describes: one per community, its own DID, the
only holder of the community's forge credentials, serving exactly one
VTC over the git-ns/bridge/{job,result,event} Trust Tasks.

- Wire: payload types generated from the specs (trust-tasks-rs 0.22
  specs::git_ns). Every inbound document is checked issuer (the one VTC,
  before any DID is resolved), transport sender, recipient, freshness,
  then its Data Integrity proof, and only then parsed. Every outbound one
  is signed (eddsa-jcs-2022, trust-tasks-proof).
- Jobs: a durable ledger gives jobId idempotency (a repeat is answered,
  a finished one has its result resent, other content is jobIdReused) and
  exactly one result per job; results and events are retried until the
  VTC acknowledges them. Each kind maps onto the Forge trait with
  ForgeHooks around it; begin* jobs answer with `next` and complete
  through the forge's redirect or the device flow, event then result.
- State: one redb file; secrets sealed with AES-256-GCM under a mounted
  master key. Namespaces (capabilities, CapabilityChanged), GitHub managed
  sets and required-workflow pins are restored into the adapters on start;
  Forgejo bot tokens rotate mint -> persist -> retire.
- Transport: DIDComm through the mediator (the TDK's ATM and delivery
  layer), keeping the authcrypt sender and never flushing the inbox.
- HTTP (axum): GitHub manifest registration, App setup, webhooks; Forgejo
  OAuth redirects and webhooks. Body limits; signatures before parsing.
- The bridge-posted check (GitHub fallback): pull_request / merge_group
  webhooks -> the commits fetched as objects into a throwaway bare repo
  with a read-only token -> verify-trust as a library (qualified resource,
  namespace as fallback) -> "Verify commit trust" completed as the App.

Dockerfile, example config and docs/BRIDGE.md (operator guide).

title: feat(vgi-forge-github): the bridge posts the check where no required workflow can
body:
feat(vgi-forge-github): the bridge posts the check where no required workflow can

Outside an org required workflow a check pinned to the GitHub Actions App
is forgeable: a workflow on another branch can post a passing "Verify
commit trust" run onto someone else's pull request. Per the design's
decision on forged check runs (§9), the bridge now runs verify-trust
itself and posts the check as the community's App.

- GitHubConfig::with_bridge_checks: in namespaces without a required
  workflow the plan commits no workflow (and removes an old one), and the
  ruleset pins the required check to the App's own integration id.
- inspect counts only a check pinned to that App and reports the new
  CheckSourceGuard::BridgePosted; Capabilities gains bridge_posted_check.
- checks module: parse_check_trigger (pull_request, merge_group; the
  signature is verified before the body is read), compare_commits,
  contents_read_token, clone_url, start/finish_check_run, each with a
  token for the one repository and the one permission it needs.
- The manifest asks for checks:write and the pull_request and
  merge_group events, with the rationale next to the permission.

- **`community-manager/README.md`:** replaces "the current OpenVTC initial-days default is two-VRC" with: OpenVTC does not prescribe a join policy; the joining guide shows open requests (what its walkthrough uses) and a two-VRC example.

title: Guard the explore guide's pinned release in CI
body:
Refs #40

The explore guide has operators download `setup-explore.sh` from a tagged release and check it against a SHA-256 pinned on the page, because they then run it as root. Nothing checks that pin, so two failures are invisible:

- **drift** — the pin stops describing the script in the tree, and the guide tells operators to reject the current release;
- **missing** — the pinned release was never published, so both downloads 404 and the explore stream stops at its first command.

The second is the state of `main` today, and is what #40 reports.

`guard-release-pin.sh` covers both. It takes the version, the hash **and the download URL** from `sysop/explore/01-server-setup.md` itself rather than restating any of them, so it checks the URL operators are actually told to fetch — the same approach `guard-remote-exec.sh` takes of grepping the real pages.

**Why the triggers are split.** `RELEASING.md` deliberately pins the version and hash in a merged PR *before* the tag that publishes the release exists. A guard demanding the release on every pull request would block the very PR that makes the release possible. So:

| check | trigger | today |
| --- | --- | --- |
| pin matches `scripts/setup-explore.sh` | every PR, push, schedule | passes |
| pinned release is published and matches | push to `main` + daily cron | **fails until `v1.0.0` is tagged** |

**That second failure is intentional and is the point.** It is the bug in #40 becoming visible; it goes green when the tag is pushed, with no further change here. If you would rather land the tag first and this after, say so and I will hold it.

### Verified

`shellcheck scripts/*.sh .github/scripts/*.sh` — clean, exit 0, all three scripts (shellcheck 0.11.0).

Behaviour, exercised against a local HTTP server standing in for the release:

| case | result |
| --- | --- |
| pin matches the tree | passes |
| pinned release absent (real `v1.0.0`) | fails, names the tag and points at RELEASING.md |
| script edited, pin not re-pinned | fails, prints both hashes |
| `VER=` or `SHA256=` missing from the guide | fails |
| release published and matching | passes |
| published asset does not match the pin | fails, prints both hashes |
| release `SHA256SUMS` disagrees with its own asset | fails |

The guide is read with `tr -d '\r'` so a checkout made with `core.autocrlf=true` parses the same way the runner does. The script hash itself is deliberately taken from the file as it stands, matching what `release.yml` hashes.
author: mitchuski

title: Fetch the explore setup script from main and drop the release flow
body:
Closes #40. Supersedes #43.

The explore guide had operators download `setup-explore.sh` from a tagged release, check it against a SHA-256 pinned on the page, and verify a build provenance attestation. The pin, the release assets and the attestation all come from github.com over TLS and are all controlled by whoever can write to this repository, so together they add little over fetching the script from the repository itself.

What they did add:

- a pin-before-tag release process (`RELEASING.md`) that is easy to leave half-done, and was: `v1.0.0` was pinned but never tagged, so Step 3 has 404'd since #37 (#40);
- a `gh` 2.49+ requirement for the attestation check, which Ubuntu 26.04's `gh` 2.46 does not meet;
- the CI guard proposed in #43 to keep the pin and the release in step.

For a stream that sets up a throwaway VM, that is more process than protection.

### Changes

- **`sysop/explore/01-server-setup.md` Step 3:** download the script from `main` to a file, read it, run it. The `VER`/`SHA256` pin, the hash checks and the attestation step are removed.
- **`scripts/setup-explore.sh`:** header comment updated to match (comment only).
- **`.github/scripts/guard-remote-exec.sh`:** the check against fetching from `main` is removed. The pipe-to-shell and `bash <(curl …)` checks stay, so the guide still has to download to a file rather than pipe into `bash`.
- **Removed:** `RELEASING.md` and `.github/workflows/release.yml`.

### Trade-off

Every merge to `main` now reaches operators immediately, and nothing pins the script's hash. Review of changes to `setup-explore.sh` is the control.

### After merge

- Close #43.
- Delete the `release` environment under Settings → Environments, if it was created.

### Verified

- `shellcheck scripts/setup-explore.sh .github/scripts/guard-remote-exec.sh`: clean.
- `markdownlint-cli2 "**/*.md"`: 0 issues.
- `guard-remote-exec.sh`: passes.
author: geoffturk

title: Explore Step 3 pins release `v1.0.0`, which was never published — the setup script cannot be downloaded
body:
## What happens

`sysop/explore/01-server-setup.md` Step 3 has the operator download `setup-explore.sh` from a tagged release before running it as root:

```bash
VER=v1.0.0
SHA256=c59f53c74f423327a233bb3178651bf7958449efd88df05df8c2f8d179db1340
curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/OpenVTC/vti-setup/releases/download/${VER}/setup-explore.sh"
curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/OpenVTC/vti-setup/releases/download/${VER}/SHA256SUMS"
```

There is no `v1.0.0` release. Both URLs 404, and `-f` makes `curl` exit non-zero, so the operator finishes Step 3 with no script, no `SHA256SUMS`, and no message saying why. The explore stream stops at its first command, and the guide's own instruction — "Do not run a copy from the `main` branch" — leaves no documented way forward.

Measured 2026-09-22:

```
404  https://github.com/OpenVTC/vti-setup/releases/download/v1.0.0/setup-explore.sh
404  https://github.com/OpenVTC/vti-setup/releases/download/v1.0.0/SHA256SUMS
```

Tags on this repository:

| tag | published | assets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Banyan` | 2026-06-23 | none |
| `archive/sysop-deploy` | — | — |

## The pin is right; the release is missing

This is not a stale hash. `c59f53c7…db1340` is exactly the SHA-256 of `scripts/setup-explore.sh` as it stands on `main`, and the script has not changed since #37 introduced both the verification flow and the pin:

```
$ git show HEAD:scripts/setup-explore.sh | sha256sum
c59f53c74f423327a233bb3178651bf7958449efd88df05df8c2f8d179db1340  -

$ git log --oneline 632747b..HEAD -- scripts/setup-explore.sh
(no output)
```

So `RELEASING.md` step 2 — "Open a PR that sets `VER` and `SHA256` in Step 3 … Merge it." — landed as #37. Step 3, pushing the `v1.0.0` tag that runs `release.yml` and attaches the assets, did not. The guide has been pointing at a release that does not exist since 12 September.

## Why nothing caught it

Nothing checks the pin. `lint.yml` runs `shellcheck` and `guard-remote-exec.sh`; the guard proves no page pipes a download into a shell or fetches from `main`, which is the right property, but it says nothing about whether the pinned release resolves. A guide can therefore instruct a root operator to download from a URL that 404s and every gate in the repo stays green.

Both halves of the verification story are currently unobservable in CI:

- **the pin can drift from the script** — nothing asserts `SHA256` still matches `scripts/setup-explore.sh`, so a future PR touching the script leaves the guide pinning the old hash;
- **the pinned release can be absent** — as it is now.

## Suggested fix

Two parts, only one of which is a code change:

1. **Push the `v1.0.0` tag** so `release.yml` attaches `setup-explore.sh` and `SHA256SUMS` and records the provenance attestation. The hash in the guide is already correct for the current script, so no doc change is needed and `RELEASING.md`'s requirement that the pinning PR not touch the script is satisfied.

2. **Guard the pin in CI**, in the same shape as `guard-remote-exec.sh`, so neither half can go unobserved again. I'll open a PR for this. Two checks on different triggers, because `RELEASING.md` deliberately pins *before* the tag exists:
   - on every pull request — the pinned `SHA256` equals `sha256sum scripts/setup-explore.sh` in the tree under review. This is the drift check, and it passes today.
   - on push to `main` and on a daily schedule — the pinned `VER` release exists and its `setup-explore.sh` asset hashes to the pinned value. This is the check that would have caught the present state, and it will fail until (1) is done.

Splitting the triggers keeps the release-existence check from blocking the pinning PR that `RELEASING.md` asks for, while still turning a never-cut release into a visible failure within a day rather than a silent 404 for a sysop.

Happy to take the guard as a PR; (1) needs a maintainer.

title: security(auth)!: retire the superseded refresh token when a DID logs in again
body:
Rotation makes a stolen refresh token worth one use, and reuse detection notices it when it's reused. Neither could see a token that is never presented twice.

`/auth/` is keyed per DID and overwrites `session:{did}`, but the reverse index is a separate `refresh:{hash}` row per token, and `/auth/refresh` authorizes from that index alone — it never consults `session.refresh_token`. A login that merely added its own index row left the previous one live, so one account carried two working chains that shared no token: each refreshed into its own successor, no replay ever occurred, and detection never fired. A token stolen before a re-login kept working indefinitely and silently, alongside its owner's, and the one recovery step a user can take unaided — logging in again — did nothing to it.

`handle_authenticate` now retires the outgoing token. It reads the prior session's `refresh_token` before `store_session` overwrites the row, removes that token's index entry with the atomic claim-and-delete (so two racing logins cannot both retire it, preserving VTI-SES-030), and leaves a tombstone in its place. Ordered after the new chain is durable, as on the rotation path; both writes log on error rather than failing a login that has already committed and minted its tokens.

`RefreshTombstone` gains `cause` to record why a token was retired. `Superseded` is excluded from the innocent-retry grace window on purpose: that concession applies to a lost-rotation response, and a client that has just logged in holds its replacement. Honoring a replay there would have handed the new token to whoever replayed a pre-login theft — strictly worse than closing the gap.

Replaying a superseded token is refused and audited as `AuthAuditEvent::RefreshSuperseded` (`warn!`, `security_alert = true`), but the session is left running. Unlike reuse, the presented token is already dead — the login took its index — so revoking adds nothing against a thief, while the ordinary cause is a second device still holding what it was issued before the user signed in elsewhere. Killing the session there would sign out the client that is demonstrably current, and the re-login it forces would set the same trap again. The event still carries `security_alert` because a pre-login theft and a stale device are indistinguishable from the node's side; only an operator correlating them can say which it was.

`cleanup_expired_sessions` now also sweeps `refresh:` entries where the session no longer exists. Retirement fixes new logins but cannot reach entries already written, and those rows carry no TTL and are not inert: an orphan resolves again as soon as its DID has a session row, so it outlives a revocation and returns at the next login. The sweep is safe against a concurrent login or rotation because every writer stores the session row before its index entry, so an entry that disagrees with its row is stale rather than half-written.

Also in this change: `RefreshReuseDetected` takes its `did` from the tombstone, so the alert names the account on the `SessionGone` path where the session row is absent by definition; the lost-response retry log carries `audit = true`, since a stable session id had left it indistinguishable from an ordinary rotation; and the module header no longer describes a delete-and-recreate the handler stopped doing.

`refresh_reuse_grace` stays at 30s, now documented as a starting point rather than a ceiling — a client only discovers a lost response when its own HTTP timeout fires, so a deployment whose clients retry later than that may want 60s. It is a user-experience call, not a security one: the successor-unspent condition, not the clock, is what keeps the concession narrow. `0` still disables it entirely.

Compatibility:

* `RefreshTombstone` gains `cause` and `did`; struct-literal construction must name them. Both are `#[serde(default)]`, so stored records keep decoding — one written before these fields reads as `Rotated` with an empty `did`, the conservative reading.
* `SessionStore::store_refresh_tombstone` takes `&RefreshTombstone` instead of five positional parameters. Two adjacent `String`s and two adjacent `u64`s meant a caller could transpose `rotated_at`/`ttl` — or `session_id`/`did` — and still compile. The default impl remains a no-op, so an out-of-tree store is unaffected beyond the signature.
* `AuthAuditEvent::RefreshSuperseded` is new. `AuthAuditEvent` is `#[non_exhaustive]`, so an existing wildcard arm already covers it.
* Behavioral: a refresh token from before a re-login now returns 401 instead of minting into a parallel chain. A client that relied on the old token surviving a second login must use the newest login's token.

Implements RFC 9700 §4.14.2.

Verified: `cargo fmt --all --check`; clippy clean across vti-common, vta-service and vtc-service with `--all-targets`; 4070 tests passing over 101 suites.

title: feat(vgi-forge-github): the PR can no longer satisfy its own check (F3)
body:
feat(vgi-forge-github): the PR can no longer satisfy its own check (F3)

The generated verify-trust workflow ran on pull_request, so it ran from
the PR's own files: a writer could edit it (or add a job named "Verify
commit trust") to pass. Pinning the check to the Actions App did not help.

- Organisations with org rulesets: the workflow lives in a public,
  bridge-managed `<org>/.vgi` (itself protected by a ruleset), and an org
  ruleset ("VGI required workflow": workflows rule pinned to a commit SHA,
  enforced on creation, ~DEFAULT_BRANCH, the bridge's managed repos by id,
  active, no bypass) requires it. DIDs are literals and the web-flow
  keyring is embedded. The ruleset is read-modify-written under a
  per-namespace lock and read back; name/property conditions are rewritten
  to ids. Repos moving from the fallback get their in-repo workflow,
  variables and status-check rule cleaned up.
- Elsewhere: two or more owners get CODEOWNERS for `/.github/` (in the
  CODEOWNERS GitHub reads, keeping existing rules) plus one code-owner
  approval, dismissed on push and never the last pusher's; a solo repo gets
  the check alone (user decision). DIDs are literals; legacy variables are
  removed.
- Availability probed at bind / detect_required_workflow; only a plan
  refusal falls back, returned as ForgeError::CapabilityChanged.
- inspect reports as critical drift: org ruleset / `.vgi` weakened or the
  pin unknown or unreachable; CODEOWNERS missing, not last, naming other
  than the owners, or with GitHub-reported errors; review rule weakened;
  Actions disabled or restricted. diff holds the guard to the owner count.
- Manifest requests organization_administration: write.
- README / RUNBOOK §4, §4a: the protection and its limits, including that
  outside a required workflow repo writers are trusted not to forge check
  runs, and the untested Actions-disabled behaviour.

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.22.3
body:
### Added

- **git-ns**: Add the git namespaces specification family ([#621](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/621))

* feat(git-ns): add the git namespaces specification family

  A VTC can say today that a DID may sign commits for an org or a repo, and
  nothing else about git: who owns a repository, who may create one, who may
  merge and who may grant commit rights all live on the forge, and drift from
  the VTC as soon as someone clicks a button. git-ns makes the VTC the source of
  truth for all of it. Rights are per resource, not per role; the Trust Registry
  is the published projection verifiers read, and the forge is the enforced one.

  Five rights, spelled as the TRQP actions the VTC publishes them under:
  git.ns.admin, git.repo.create, git.repo.own, git.repo.maintain and
  git.commit.sign. Resources are forge-qualified and lowercase
  (github.com/acme/widgets, codeberg.org/acme), so a right never crosses forges
  and a community can host where it likes.

  Member- and admin-facing tasks, addressed to the VTC:

  - git-ns/namespace/bind, git-ns/namespace/unbind
  - git-ns/repo/create, git-ns/repo/adopt, git-ns/repo/transfer,
    git-ns/repo/archive
  - git-ns/right/grant, git-ns/right/revoke
  - git-ns/view
  - git-ns/account/link, git-ns/account/link-status

  git-ns/right/grant carries the family's rights model: implied rights, the
  grant-authority table, and six fixed rules a VTC enforces in its own code
  before policy runs, which policy can narrow and never loosen: scope
  containment, no escalation, the last-owner invariant, a last-admin invariant,
  the members-only floor for namespace rights, and policy-may-only-narrow. Each
  refusal has its own error code, declared once at the family level (git-ns:*).

  VTC <-> bridge tasks, for the per-community service that holds the forge
  credentials and the forge adapters:

  - git-ns/bridge/job — seven convergent, forge-neutral job kinds
  - git-ns/bridge/result — exactly one per job, per-step outcomes
  - git-ns/bridge/event — nine forge-neutral event types plus drift

  Shared shapes (resources, namespaces, RepoSummary, RightRecord, drift) live in
  git-ns/_shared/0.1.

  Bindings regenerated for Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart; conformance checks
  agree. trust-tasks-rs gains a git-ns feature, in all-specs.

| Package | Registry | Version | Bump |

| `trust-tasks-rs` | crates.io | `0.22.2` → `0.22.3` | patch |
| `trust-tasks-tsp` | crates.io | `0.22.2` → `0.22.3` | patch |
| `@openvtc/trust-tasks` | npm | `0.20.2` → `0.20.3` | patch |
| `github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/trust-tasks-go` | Go (tag `trust-tasks-go/v0.2.3`) | `0.2.2` → `0.2.3` | patch |
| `trust_tasks` | pub.dev | `0.2.2` → `0.2.3` | patch |

What merging does, per registry (all in `publish.yml`, each keyed on "this
version is not published yet"):

- **crates.io** — `release-plz-release` tags `<crate>-v<version>`, publishes in
  dependency order and creates a GitHub Release per crate. Bump levels come from
  `cargo-semver-checks`.
- **npm** — `publish-npm` publishes with OIDC provenance and tags
  `<prefix>-v<version>`.
- **Go** — `publish-go` builds, vets and tests, then pushes the tag, which *is*
  the publication. **Irreversible**: proxy.golang.org never forgets a tag.
- **pub.dev** — `tag-dart` verifies against the *published* core and pushes the
  tag; `publish-dart.yml` publishes from it.

The npm, Go and Dart bumps are only as accurate as the commit subjects — nothing
checks their APIs the way `cargo-semver-checks` checks the crates. Look for a
missing `!` before merging.

This branch is regenerated from `main` on every push, so do not commit to it —
edits are force-pushed away. See RELEASING.md.

title: fix(forge-forgejo): address the PR #64 review
body:
fix(forge-forgejo): address the PR #64 review

- Rotation is two-phase. `mint_token` identifies the token in use (by the
  id it recorded, else an unambiguous last-eight match) before minting,
  mints, verifies and swaps, and hands the new secret back for the caller
  to persist; nothing can fail after the swap. `retire_token` then deletes
  exactly the one named token, never a `vgi-bridge-*` pattern, so replicas
  and people sharing the bot keep theirs. `rotate_token` is gone.
- Rule shadowing: Forgejo applies the first matching rule, comparing plain
  names case-insensitively. Another plain rule named like the default
  branch is reported (`covers_default_branch: false`, bypass
  `shadowing-rule:<name>`), and the protection step refuses to run past
  it; a default branch with glob characters is refused.
- Account-link state is MACed with a hash of the member DID and checked
  against the member the caller names; a link completed into another
  session fails. Not single-use without a store (documented).
- Check names and the configured status context may not contain glob
  characters, which Forgejo would read as a pattern and drop if invalid.
- A rule with the merge allow-list off reports `merge: everyone with
  write access` as a bypass actor.
- A same-named team is adopted only if empty or holding just the bot.
- `refresh_plan` / `refresh_managed_files`: open the managed rule to the
  bot alone (pushes on, push allow-list = bot, protected files cleared),
  write the files, restore the exact prior settings and read them back —
  always attempting the restore, failing loudly if it did not hold. The
  workflow header, README and RUNBOOK say how protected files change.
- CI: the Forgejo image is pinned by digest in
  `tests/forgejo/Dockerfile`, which the test and the job read and
  Dependabot's docker ecosystem watches; the job has `timeout-minutes`.
- Live test: adding `.forgejo/workflows/sub/x.yaml` and deleting the
  workflows directory are refused too; the refresh and two-phase rotation
  run live. README notes that a same-repo PR's workflow token can post
  statuses as well.

title: Two links 404 on GitHub, and CI does not run the documented markdown lint
body:
Two small things found while reading the developer journey. Both are one PR; happy to send it.

## 1. `developer/01-personal-vta.md` links to `/sysop/…`, which GitHub resolves off the site root

Two links are root-absolute:

```
developer/01-personal-vta.md:4:  **Tested on:** [Ubuntu Server](/sysop/explore/01-server-setup.md)
developer/01-personal-vta.md:96: Complete the [Ubuntu Server](/sysop/explore/01-server-setup.md) deployment before continuing…
```

A leading `/` in rendered markdown resolves against `github.com`, not the repository, so both land on `https://github.com/sysop/explore/01-server-setup.md` — 404 (measured 2026-09-22). Line 96 is in **Prerequisites**, so the first thing the guide asks a developer to do is follow a dead link.

Every other reference in the repo already uses the relative form, including the sibling index:

```
developer/README.md:19:  see [Explore 01 — Server Setup](../sysop/explore/01-server-setup.md) in sysop
sysop/explore/02-walkthrough.md:18:  Complete the [01 — Server setup](01-server-setup.md) first.
```

Fix: `../sysop/explore/01-server-setup.md` in both places. These are the only two broken relative links in the repo — I checked every one.

## 2. `markdownlint-cli2` is configured and documented, but never runs in CI

`CLAUDE.md` names the lint step:

```bash
markdownlint-cli2 "**/*.md"
```

and `.markdownlint.json` is committed (MD013 off, MD024 siblings-only). But `lint.yml` has one job, `shell`, running `shellcheck` and `guard-remote-exec.sh`. Nothing lints the markdown — in a repository whose `CLAUDE.md` opens "a documentation-only repository — no build system, no tests, no application code".

The tree is already clean, so this adds a guard and repairs nothing:

```
$ npx markdownlint-cli2 "**/*.md"
markdownlint-cli2 v0.23.3 (markdownlint v0.41.1)
Linting: 14 files
Summary: 0 issues in 0 files
```

Fix: a `markdown` job in `lint.yml` alongside `shell`, pinned the same way the checkout action already is.

---

Neither of these changes any instruction or any behaviour — link targets and a CI job only. Filing them together because they are both one-line housekeeping; say the word if you would rather have them separate.

- A DID clicked anywhere in the console (ACL subjects, audit actors,
  credential issuers and holders, transports, contexts, the whoami

title: fix: send every VTC-bound Trust Task in the DIDComm binding envelope (Keyring VTI-42)
body:
## Why

**Keyring VTI-42** (Berkman Center Keyring wallet) reported that the VTC accepted Trust Tasks over DIDComm typed as their own task URI. **VTI #1687** (merged) fixed that on the VTC: per the Trust Tasks DIDComm binding (`bindings/didcomm/0.2` §2–§4), a Trust Task over DIDComm **MUST** be carried with DIDComm `type` = `https://trusttasks.org/binding/didcomm/0.1/envelope` (the constant `vti_common::capability_client::TRUST_TASK_ENVELOPE_TYPE`, re-exported here as `openvtc_core::capabilities::TRUST_TASK_ENVELOPE_TYPE`), with the task document as the body. The twelve legacy task-typed arms are gone, so a VTC now answers a task-typed message with a `BAD_REQUEST` problem-report naming the envelope type.

Joins, self-removal, the member VMC and capability toggles already sent the envelope. These did not, and against a post-#1687 VTC every one of them is refused:

| Send site | Task |
|---|---|
| `vetting::wire::to_message` (via `sign_and_send`) | `vtc/join-requests/manifest/0.2` (TUI join flow + vetting pane) |
| same | `vetting/vetters/list/0.1`, `vetters/profile/0.1`, `vetters/resend/0.1` |
| same | `vetting/revoke-statement/0.1` |
| `personhood::Route::send` (DIDComm arm) | `vtc/members/personhood/challenge/0.1`, `…/assert/0.1` |

No VTA-bound Trust Task is sent task-typed; the VTA path goes through `vta-sdk`, which already envelopes.

## What changed

- **Outbound.** `wire::to_message` picks the carriage per document: `is_community_bound(type)` → envelope, else the task URI. Personhood's DIDComm arm always envelopes (a small `didcomm_request` helper, unit-tested). The TSP arms are untouched — they already use the TSP binding envelope.
- **Dual reply matching.** `didcomm::open_didcomm_envelope` (the DIDComm twin of `tsp_document_to_message`) runs at the top of `process_inbound_message`: an envelope-typed message is re-typed as the document it carries (`thid` = the message's, else the document's `threadId`; `from` stays the authcrypt sender; body unchanged). Every existing handler therefore receives a reply the same way whether the VTC types it as the response document (what it sends today — VTI #1687 deliberately left `tt_didcomm_reply` that way until this consumer could read the envelope) or as the envelope (what binding §5 requires, and a follow-up VTC PR will switch to). Correlation is unchanged: by `thid` / document `threadId`.
- **Capability replies** are now read in both carriages too. Previously only the envelope-typed form was handled, and the document-typed form (`governance/capability/*#response`, what the VTC actually sends) was dropped at the inbound gate. The gate pattern and `inbound_gate_census` now include `governance/capability/*`. A `trust-task-error` is offered to the capability view *and* falls through, since it may refuse anything.
- **Problem-report → typed failure.** A DIDComm problem-report threaded on a pending vetting question (or application / withdrawal) now produces `CommunityAnswer::Refused` immediately, via the same path a `trust-task-error` takes, instead of waiting out the query timeout. Unmatched reports still fall through to the join handler.

## Peer legs — deliberately not moved

`vetting/request`, `session`, `decline` and their responses go openvtc ↔ openvtc. A released openvtc routes those on the DIDComm `type`, so enveloping them on the send side alone would silently drop every request a not-yet-updated vetter receives. They stay task-typed. This PR adds the *receiving* half (enveloped peer documents open and route), so a later release can switch the sends once this one is the floor.

## Tests

- New unit tests: community-bound vs peer carriage in `wire`; personhood envelope; `open_didcomm_envelope` mapping (typ/thid/body/from, non-envelope and untyped cases); vetter-list answers and refusals read in **both** carriages; a threaded problem-report refuses the pending question, an unthreaded one is left for the join handler. The existing profile round-trip test now opens the enveloped request the way the VTC does.
- `cargo test --workspace -- --include-ignored` (includes the mediator-backed `vetting_e2e` / `join_lifecycle_e2e` suites): all pass.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --all --check`: clean.
- Not run: a live round trip against a VTC built from VTI `origin/main`. openvtc has no VTC harness (its e2e suites stand a mediator profile in for the community). The envelope shape sent is the one the join/members/capability sends already use against the VTC's `envelope_task_handler`, which reads the DIDComm body as the document.

## Pre-merge checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2) — no new clients
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1) — unchanged
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4) — no retries added
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6) — n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*) — carriage change only; conforms to the binding the VTC now enforces
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*) — n/a
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*) — a DIDComm-layer refusal is now surfaced as a refusal instead of a timeout (R6.4)
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1) — no new mutations
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers — none

title: feat(git-ns): add the git namespaces specification family (#621)
body:
feat(git-ns): add the git namespaces specification family (#621)

* feat(git-ns): add the git namespaces specification family

A VTC can say today that a DID may sign commits for an org or a repo, and
nothing else about git: who owns a repository, who may create one, who may
merge and who may grant commit rights all live on the forge, and drift from
the VTC as soon as someone clicks a button. git-ns makes the VTC the source of
truth for all of it. Rights are per resource, not per role; the Trust Registry
is the published projection verifiers read, and the forge is the enforced one.

Five rights, spelled as the TRQP actions the VTC publishes them under:
git.ns.admin, git.repo.create, git.repo.own, git.repo.maintain and
git.commit.sign. Resources are forge-qualified and lowercase
(github.com/acme/widgets, codeberg.org/acme), so a right never crosses forges
and a community can host where it likes.

Member- and admin-facing tasks, addressed to the VTC:

- git-ns/namespace/bind, git-ns/namespace/unbind
- git-ns/repo/create, git-ns/repo/adopt, git-ns/repo/transfer,
  git-ns/repo/archive
- git-ns/right/grant, git-ns/right/revoke
- git-ns/view
- git-ns/account/link, git-ns/account/link-status

git-ns/right/grant carries the family's rights model: implied rights, the
grant-authority table, and six fixed rules a VTC enforces in its own code
before policy runs, which policy can narrow and never loosen: scope
containment, no escalation, the last-owner invariant, a last-admin invariant,
the members-only floor for namespace rights, and policy-may-only-narrow. Each
refusal has its own error code, declared once at the family level (git-ns:*).

VTC <-> bridge tasks, for the per-community service that holds the forge
credentials and the forge adapters:

- git-ns/bridge/job — seven convergent, forge-neutral job kinds
- git-ns/bridge/result — exactly one per job, per-step outcomes
- git-ns/bridge/event — nine forge-neutral event types plus drift

Shared shapes (resources, namespaces, RepoSummary, RightRecord, drift) live in
git-ns/_shared/0.1.

Bindings regenerated for Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart; conformance checks
agree. trust-tasks-rs gains a git-ns feature, in all-specs.

title: vtc: the admin console cannot sign, so every bearer route #1641 would retire has to stay
body:
Design note: [`docs/05-design-notes/vtc-console-signing.md`](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/blob/main/docs/05-design-notes/vtc-console-signing.md). Read it before starting — this issue is the work list, not the reasoning.

## Why

#1681 moved the first four admin member verbs onto the signed-document dispatcher and kept their bearer routes, because **the admin console cannot author a signed Trust Task document**. `vtc-trust-task-proof-enforcement.md` §6b states that as the removal point for every bearer route in the #1641 migration. The console is the only one of the three blocking client surfaces (admin SPA, `cnm`, `vtc-client`) with no path at all, and it is the largest share: **34 of the 49** bearer-served proof-REQUIRED tasks are console-reachable, including all four #1681 kept.

Premise verified: `vtc-service/admin-ui/src` has no signing primitive outside generated OpenAPI doc comments, and no crypto dependency. The passkey cannot substitute — the `webauthn-vti-v1` cryptosuite that would have let a WebAuthn assertion *be* a Data-Integrity proof was superseded in this repo on 2026-05-20.

## The shape

**A console signing key is a credential of the operator's existing admin DID, the way a passkey is** — not an identity of its own. The operator already *is* a DID with an `acl:<did>` row; that DID is a `did:key`, so it cannot grow a second verification method, and #1658's `Invariant::SelfPromotion` (VTI-OPS-050) blocks giving the console key its own admin ACL row. So the VTC stores a **delegation**: "console key K may act as admin DID D", enrolled by D behind the step-up the console already runs, listed beside the passkeys, individually revocable, conferring no role on its own.

Authority stays an ACL row read at execution time, so #1681's stated property (`admin_signer` never consults `sessions_ks`) survives.

Server-side signing is **rejected**, not deferred — VTI-OPS-021 / -093. See §5E.

## Decisions needed before starting

1. **Option A or B** — durable per-device delegation (recommended) vs ephemeral key bound via the already-plumbed `session_pubkey_b58btc` (materially cheaper, authority returns through the session, forward-compatible).
2. **Browser-support floor.** WebCrypto Ed25519 (Chrome 137+ / Firefox 130+ / Safari 17+) buys a non-extractable key; `@noble/curves` works everywhere but the key is extractable by definition.
3. **May an operator sign from two devices?** The note assumes yes, N delegations per admin DID, mirroring passkeys.
4. **Default delegation lifetime**, and whether a key survives sign-out.

## Work, assuming A

- [ ] **Client signing module.** Lift `affinidi-webvh-service/did-hosting-ui/lib/session-key.ts` (zero-dependency, already implements the construction) with three changes: `extractable: false` + an assertion, per-origin IndexedDB record, `created` back-dated 60 s. Sign at the `src/lib/api.ts` seam, not at call sites.
- [ ] **JCS conformance test** — round-trip each dispatched payload's canonical form against Rust `serde_jcs`. The lifted canonicaliser is "good enough for our documents", not conformance-tested (number serialisation, Unicode normalisation).
- [ ] **`console_keys` keyspace** — `console_key:<consoleDid>` → `{ admin_did, label, created_at, created_by, expires_at, last_used_at }`. Classify in the backup census (`EXCLUDED_FROM_BACKUP` — a restore must not resurrect a browser's signing authority). Sweeper tick for `expires_at`.
- [ ] **Enrolment verbs** mirroring `auth/passkey/{enroll,revoke}`: `POST /v1/admin/console-keys` (`AdminAuth` + live `StepUpAuth`), `GET`, `DELETE /{consoleDid}`. Needs an upstream Trust Task spec in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf before it can be dispatched — see `new-task-family-needs-upstream-spec-first`.
- [ ] **`admin_signer` delegation step** — signer's own ACL row first (unchanged), then the delegation → the delegating admin's ACL row, at execution time.
- [ ] **Audit carries both** the admin DID (actor) and the console DID (acting credential), via `AuditLogEntry.detail`.
- [ ] **Console UI** — "enable signing for this browser" + a key list beside `myPasskeys.tsx`; graceful degradation to the bearer path when unsupported or not yet enrolled.
- [ ] **Keep the step-up where it is.** A console key is possession of a browser profile; the passkey is possession of an authenticator plus UV. Admin-conferring verbs on the signed door must still consult `elevation::verified` on the delegating admin's live session.
- [ ] **Retire the four #1681 kept** — move `plugins/members.tsx` to `POST /v1/trust-tasks`, check `members/update`'s `extensions` bag against the signed door's **64 KiB** cap (vs 1 MB on the bearer chain), give `vtc-client` the same path, delete routes + OpenAPI entries, regenerate `openapi.json` + `wire.ts`.

## Follow-ups

- [ ] Report upstream to `affinidi-webvh-service`: `did-hosting-ui/lib/session-key.ts` passes `extractable: true` to `generateKey` on the stated reasoning that it is needed to export the raw public key. It is not — WebCrypto sets `publicKey.[[extractable]]` unconditionally and `privateKey.[[extractable]]` from the argument — so the session private key is exportable by any script in the origin. One-character fix. Measured table in §4b of the note.
- [ ] **Where this should end up** (§7): if the operator's admin identity were a `did:webvh` rather than a `did:key`, the console key would be published as a verification method in the operator's own DID document, `issuer` would be the admin DID, and the delegation record would disappear — along with the objection that it is not publicly readable. Larger change; should not gate this one.

title: Round 2: hidden vetting (024), 023 amended, formal models, guide split (WG-13)
body:
Round 2, stacked on #11 (base `review-2026-09-21`; it retargets to `main` when #11 merges). Four commits:

1. **WG-13: the explanatory chapters move to the companion Implementation Guide.** Cryptographic Background, Implementation Guide, Trust-Graph Operations and Research and Book become short pointers to the guide in `trustoverip/dtgwg-zkp-tf`, as the chair's Round 1 position asked (refine 2). Construction records, public inputs, integration and conformance stay here. The guide contribution should merge and publish first, so the pointers resolve.
2. **An optional `formal` part on construction records.** Schema, renderer ("Formal verification" block) and validator rules; an incomplete part, or one naming no hypotheses, is refused. A formal part confers no evidence state.
3. **Round 2 records.**
   - **024, hidden-vetting admission** (new, composed): k pairwise-distinct eligible vetters of the live period attest without the community learning which. The construction named for the Linux Plumbers integration is recorded as an option until its authors publish; the lab's Groth16 route is constructed (clause 7 not built there).
   - **DG-024-4, pending review:** clause 4 admits secret-derived serials (cap each vetter) or blind-issued transferable tokens (cap the vetter set), with a `doesNotEstablish` line for the per-vetter cap.
   - **023 amended:** no witness without a relationship credential; the single-use challenge; and a `doesNotEstablish` line: no clause excludes a self-vouch by an applicant who is already a member (010 excludes it at the leaf level, 024 by clause 7). Evidence for WG-16.
   - **001 and 006:** issuance requirements the formal models showed necessary (domain separation or fixed path depth; `rl_root` over strictly sorted handles).
   - **Formal parts on seventeen records**, each with a scope line naming the clauses its model covers. They are machine-checked properties of abstract models, not implementation correspondence; the Lean sources are local until an immutable evidence revision is cited.
   - **007:** Denys Popov's review recorded as *refined* (did:key has no space for the commitment; did:peer numalgo 2/4, did:web, did:webvh can carry one).

4. **Record 013 specified — mutual edge admissibility (cred-spec #25).** From `requested` to `specified`: each party learns the counterparty's committed half would be admitted under its own community's published policy, and neither half is revealed until both answers are yes. Composed from 022 (commit before either answer), 001 twice (the form in the counterparty's policy root; a claimed membership in the prover's root) and 003. The negative space names policy privacy (policies stay published, the request's step one), fairness (a party can learn the yes and walk away) and acceptance once published. With it, every record in the draft is at `specified` or beyond, and all eighteen carry a formal model.

Checks: validator 23/23; generated sections match regeneration; conformance test passes; Spec-Up-T render clean.

title: fix(forge-forgejo): write the DIDs into the protected workflow by default
body:
fix(forge-forgejo): write the DIDs into the protected workflow by default

Forgejo gates the repository Actions-variables API on repository owner (the org's Owners team); the bot is an admin through its team, and the live test showed the variables step refused with "user should be the owner of the repo". Making the bot an org owner would be far more than it needs. The workflow is also the safer home for the DIDs: it changes only through a pull request, which the protected paths refuse, whereas an owner can re-point a variable without one. Variables stay available behind ForgejoConfig::with_actions_variables().

title: feat(vtc): the join decision and the profile edit are served as signed documents
body:
Refs #1641 — phase 2, batch 2. Follows #1681 (batch 1) and takes the pair
`docs/05-design-notes/vtc-trust-task-proof-enforcement.md` §6b named as next.

## What moved

| task | proof | issuedAt | generated types | bearer route |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `vtc/join-requests/decide/0.1` | REQUIRED | REQUIRED | payload + `#response` | `POST /v1/join-requests/{id}/decide`, **kept** |
| `vtc/community/profile/update/0.1` | REQUIRED | REQUIRED | payload + `#response` | `PUT /v1/community/profile`, **kept** |

Re-derived from `vtc-service/src/routes/mod.rs`'s bindings against each spec's
front matter in `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf` rather than taken from the brief; both
declare `proofRequirement: REQUIRED` and `issuedAtRequirement: REQUIRED`, and
both have generated payload and response types in trust-tasks-rs 0.21.21.

**Two, not three.** The third of the same shape would be
`vtc/admin/invites/{create,revoke}`, which another session owns, and `decide`
is heavy enough on its own — it is the first migrated verb that issues
credentials, so most of the review value here is in the replay argument rather
than in a third near-identical arm.

Both are now bound in `DISPATCHED_URIS` / `dispatch_typed`, reachable over
REST, DIDComm and TSP, and each route handler's body is lifted into a
transport-free inner (`decide_inner`, `update_profile_inner`) that both doors
call, so the two cannot answer differently.

## Authorization, compared door by door

Checked per task rather than assumed from batch 1.

| | bearer route | signed door |
|---|---|---|
| `decide` | `AdminAuth` — `Role::Admin`, nothing else | `admin_signer` → `acl::resolve_auth_role`, which admits only `VtcRole::Admin` |
| `profile/update` | `AdminAuth` — `Role::Admin`, nothing else | same |

So: **no super-admin bar on either** (unlike `members/purge` in batch 1),
**no context scoping on either**, and **no vetter/admin distinction** — a VTC
community is one scope, and a join request belongs to the community rather than
to a context within it. `resolve_auth_role` refuses every non-admin `VtcRole`,
so `admin_signer` returning at all *is* `AdminAuth`'s question.

The single difference is batch 1's, and it is stricter in the same direction:
the ACL row is read at execution time rather than copied into a token when the
session was minted, so an expired or removed row refuses on the signed door and
would not have refused on the bearer one. Tests hold both directions — a member
and a row-less DID are refused; a **context-scoped** admin is admitted, because
`AdminAuth` admitted them and a gate copied one notch too tight is as much a
regression as one copied too loose.

## The body-cap finding for `community/profile/update`

The signed door is the governed unauth chain: per-IP rate limit and a
**64 KiB** body cap, against 1 MB on the bearer route. §6b says to check each
batch's verbs against that rather than assume, and this is the first moved verb
carrying operator-authored content.

**64 KiB is enough.** Every field the operation accepts is capped by
`CommunityProfileUpdate::apply` *before* anything is written:

- `name` 200 characters, `description` 4 000, `contactEmail` 320
- `logoUrl` 2 048 **and** constrained to `http(s)`, so a `data:` image cannot
  ride in it at all — which is the case that would otherwise blow the cap
- `extensions` 16 KiB, measured serialised

Their sum at the worst UTF-8/escape expansion is about 44 KiB; a realistic
maximal profile is nearer 25 KiB. The document envelope and its proof add
roughly 1.5 KiB. And the cap **refuses with 413** rather than truncating, so a
large-but-valid update is never silently shortened.

Three members are *not* capped — `publicUrl`,
`personhood.governanceFrameworkUrl` and `personhood.acceptedIdvps` — so the
payload is unbounded in principle, although no legitimate value approaches
64 KiB (they are two URLs and a list of IDVP DIDs). All three are published on
the unauthenticated `/v1/community/public-profile`, which is the same
stored-payload argument the existing caps were added for; capping them is a
change to both doors' input validation and belongs in a change about that, not
in a transport migration. Flagging it rather than carrying it.

`join-requests/decide` is trivially inside the cap: `id`, an enum, and a
`reason` the route caps at 1 024 characters.

## Replay and double-issue on `decide`

This is the batch's real risk. Approving admits the applicant *and* issues a
membership credential and a role endorsement, so a decision executed twice
issues two of each and strands the first on a status-list slot the member row
no longer points at — unrevocable.

Nothing was added at the handler for it, deliberately. The spine claims the
document's `id` **before** dispatch and settles it after (§6a), so a redelivery
— the routine case, since the mediator re-pushes an undelivered inbox — is
answered with the *recorded* response and never re-enters the arm. A
handler-level "have I seen this id?" would be exactly the check-then-act the
claim exists to replace.

`vti_ops_025_a_replayed_decision_does_not_issue_a_second_credential` drives the
same document twice through the issuance path and asserts the second reply is
byte-identical to the first, that the member still holds the credential the
first execution issued, and that no second status-list slot was burned. A
re-execution would have answered `notPending` instead, so the assertion
discriminates.

The `notPending` refusal keeps its own meaning and its own test: a second,
*different* decision aimed at an already-decided request is a conflict an
operator should see, not a duplicate to absorb.

## Clients

Nothing breaks, confirmed rather than assumed — no route is removed.

- Admin SPA: `plugins/profile.tsx` (`PUT /v1/community/profile`) and
  `plugins/joinRequests.tsx` (`POST /v1/join-requests/{id}/decide`) still call
  the bearer routes, which still exist.
- `vtc-client`: `lib.rs`'s `approve`/`reject` → `decide` on the same REST path.
- `cnm-cli`: no caller of either route.
- `openapi.json` and `wire.ts` regenerated for the two `#[utoipa::path]`
  description changes; the `wire.ts` diff is comment-only, so the SPA's types
  are unchanged.

## One divergence found, pinned rather than fixed

`vtc/community/profile/update/0.1` says the nullable members may be "explicitly
set to `null` to clear them". They cannot be:
`CommunityProfileUpdate` types them `Option<Option<String>>` with no
double-option deserializer, so serde folds an explicit `null` onto the outer
`None` and the operation reads it as "leave unchanged". That is the store's
behaviour, it predates this binding, and it holds identically on the bearer
route — what this PR is answerable for is that the two doors agree, and they
do. `an_explicit_null_does_not_yet_clear_a_nullable_member` pins it so a client
does not discover it, and fixing it moves both doors at once.

## What the next batch should take

`vtc/admin/invites/{create,revoke}` — same admin-from-ACL shape, same console
dependency — once the `vtc/invitations/*` work owned elsewhere lands. Failing
that, `vtc/config/{export,import}` or
`vtc/endorsement-types/{register,delete}`. **`vtc/backup/{export,import}`
should wait**: its bodies are the one place where the 64 KiB document cap is
plainly too small, and moving it needs that decision taken first rather than
discovered.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vtc-client --no-fail-fast` (admin-UI build
  **not** skipped)
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean
- `openapi.json` regenerated with `UPDATE_OPENAPI=1`, `wire.ts` with
  `npm run wire:generate`
- The design note's dispatched-set count moves 24 → 26, asserted by
  `the_dispatched_set_declares_the_proofs_the_design_note_records`
