body:
feat(vtc): the join decision and the profile edit are served as signed documents (#1689)

#1641 phase 2, batch 2. `vtc/join-requests/decide/0.1` and
`vtc/community/profile/update/0.1` declare `proof` REQUIRED and were served
only as flat-payload REST behind a bearer JWT, so they got none of what the
document dispatcher enforces: no proof, no recipient binding, no acceptance
window, and nothing in the accepted-id record. Both are now bound in
`DISPATCHED_URIS` / `dispatch_typed`, reachable over REST, DIDComm and TSP.

Authorization is the verified signer's ACL entry, read at execution time
(`admin_signer` → `acl::resolve_auth_role`), never a bearer token — this
endpoint reads none. Checked task by task rather than copied from batch 1:
both bearer routes apply exactly `AdminAuth` and nothing further. No
super-admin bar, no context scoping, no vetter/admin split — a VTC community
is one scope, and `resolve_auth_role` admits only `VtcRole::Admin`, so
`admin_signer` returning at all is that gate. The one difference is batch 1's
and is stricter: the ACL row is read now rather than when the session was
minted, so an expired or removed row refuses here.

`decide` is the first migrated verb whose second execution would be materially
wrong rather than redundant — approving issues a membership credential and a
role endorsement, so a replayed decision would issue two of each and strand the
first on a status-list slot nothing points at. Nothing was added at the handler
for it: the spine claims the document's `id` before dispatch and settles it
after, so a redelivery is answered with the recorded response and never
re-enters the arm, and a handler-level "have I seen this?" would be the
check-then-act the claim exists to replace. The `notPending` refusal stays what
it was — the answer to a second, *different* decision on an already-decided
request.
`vti_ops_025_a_replayed_decision_does_not_issue_a_second_credential` drives the
redelivery through issuance and checks the credential and status-list slot the
member ends up holding, not only the reply.

Each route handler's body moved into a transport-free inner both doors call, so
the two cannot answer differently; `decide_inner` takes the transport label so
the audit row says which door a decision came through instead of claiming
`rest` for a document that arrived over DIDComm.

The 64 KiB cap on the signed door was checked against `profile/update` rather
than assumed: every field the operation accepts is capped before anything is
written (name 200 chars, description 4 000, logoUrl 2 048 and `http(s)`-only so
a `data:` image cannot ride in it, contactEmail 320, the extensions bag 16 KiB
measured serialised), summing to about 44 KiB at the worst encoding and nearer
25 KiB for a realistic maximal profile. So it fits, and the cap refuses with
413 rather than truncating.

Both bearer routes stay, each carrying the transitional note and its removal
point in its OpenAPI description: the admin console has no signing primitive at
all and its second factor is a passkey, which cannot produce a Data-Integrity
proof, so it holds no key with which to author a Trust Task document.

One divergence found and pinned rather than fixed: the task says the nullable
profile members may be set to `null` to clear them, and they cannot be —
`CommunityProfileUpdate` types them `Option<Option<String>>` with no
double-option deserializer, so serde folds `null` onto the outer `None` and the
update reads it as "unchanged". It is the store's behaviour, identical on both
doors, and fixing it moves both at once.

VTI-OPS-020, VTI-OPS-025, VTI-OPS-026, VTI-OPS-027.

title: feat(forge-forgejo): add the Forgejo adapter
body:
feat(forge-forgejo): add the Forgejo adapter

`vgi-forge-forgejo` implements `Forge` (and `ForgeHooks`) for a Forgejo
instance, Gitea best effort, as one community's bot user (§5.9):

- Bot token scoped to write:organization, write:repository and read:user
  (the last for the login-by-id lookup before every role change). Held
  zeroized, swappable; `rotate_token` mints, verifies, swaps and deletes
  the old tokens. Forgejo mints tokens only under basic auth, so
  unattended rotation is an explicit choice (`TokenRotation::WithPassword`);
  otherwise `replace_token` verifies an operator-minted one.
- `/api/v1/version` probing switches off fast-forward-only merges
  (Forgejo 7 / Gitea 1.22) and the Actions variables API (Forgejo 8 /
  Gitea 1.22) before a plan is built.
- Binding through OAuth2 authorisation code + PKCE: owner check via
  `/users/{u}/orgs/{org}/permissions`, `vgi-bridge` team (admin, create
  repos, all repos) with the bot in it, org webhook, admin token wiped.
  Account linking the same way. The PKCE verifier is derived from the
  state, so the adapter keeps no per-flow state.
- Roles: admin; maintain = write plus the default branch's merge
  allow-list; committer none or write. Logins looked up fresh by id.
- Bootstrap: fast-forward-only merges and Actions on (first, the step an
  old instance refuses), the workflow by full URL with version and sha256
  pinned, variables (inlined without the API), and branch protection: no
  pushes, applies to admins, the status context required, merge
  allow-list, and the workflow paths and keyring protected so no PR can
  rewrite its own check. A signing-key fallback for instances without
  fast-forward-only merges.
- Webhooks: X-Forgejo-Signature / X-Gitea-Signature, hex HMAC-SHA256,
  constant time; repository created/deleted events.

Tests: a wiremock suite for every operation, and a Docker Forgejo
integration test (`tests/forgejo_live.rs`, `#[ignore]` and gated on
VGI_FORGEJO_IT=1) that drives bind → create → bootstrap → roles →
protected workflow → archive → rotation and checks every endpoint used
against the instance's swagger; CI runs it in a `forgejo-live` job.
First crates.io publish is manual, like the other forge crates.

All additive on `#[non_exhaustive]` types; the GitHub adapter is

title: fix(vtc)!: a Trust Task over DIDComm rides the binding envelope only (Keyring VTI-42)
body:
Keyring **VTI-42** (Berkman Center Keyring wallet team): a client that sent a Trust Task over DIDComm with the DIDComm `type` set to the task URI (`…/vtc/join-requests/withdraw/0.1` to a VTC, `…/auth/whoami/0.1` to a VTA) got a problem-report reading `unsupported message type`. The same document in the binding envelope (`https://trusttasks.org/binding/didcomm/0.1/envelope`) worked.

## Root cause

The DIDComm binding (`bindings/didcomm/0.2` §2–§5) makes the envelope the **only** DIDComm carriage for a Trust Task. A consumer must refuse any other type at the DIDComm layer, and that refusal gets no `trust-task-error`. The VTC router broke this in two ways:

- It still had **12 task-typed arms** next to the envelope arm: join-requests submit, manifest 0.1 and 0.2, status, members/self-remove, members/vmc, and six vtc/vetting URIs. So 12 verbs worked in either carriage and every other served verb (withdraw, supplement, rooms/*, personhood/*) worked only in the envelope. Two of those arms, `members/self-remove` and `members/vmc`, parsed bespoke bodies and called the effect directly, **skipping `dispatch_trust_task_core`**. That meant no freshness, recipient or proof checks on that path.
- The fallback answered a Trust Task URI with a bare `unsupported message type`. That reads as "this service doesn't implement the task", which is false.

The VTA router already routes Trust Tasks only through the envelope. Only its fallback comment was misleading.

## What changed

- **VTC `messaging::route`**: removed the 12 task-typed arms and their handlers. Before deleting anything I checked that every one of these URIs is in `DISPATCHED_URIS` and served by the spine through the envelope, self-remove and vmc included (`handle_self_remove`, `handle_member_vmc`). The envelope arm now logs a refused task's code and reason, which keeps the #539 visibility that only the submit arm used to have. Dead helpers (`app_error_code`, `unauthorized_reply`, `app_error_report`) are removed.
- **VTC `unhandled_message` / VTA `handle_unknown`**: a type starting with `https://trusttasks.org/spec/` still gets a DIDComm problem-report (`e.p.msg.bad-request`). The comment now says Trust Tasks must be carried in the DIDComm binding envelope `https://trusttasks.org/binding/didcomm/0.1/envelope`. The report is threaded with `thid` = the request id. The VTA fallback now sets `thid` explicitly.
- **Parity tests driven by the dispatcher's own list**:
  - VTC `tests/didcomm_envelope_binding.rs` walks `DISPATCHED_URIS` + `vti_rooms::wire::ROOMS_DISPATCHED_URIS` through the real mediator harness. Every URI in the envelope must be answered and never answered "unsupported message type". The same URI typed as itself must get a threaded problem-report that names the envelope type and has no `trust-task-error` payload. This replaces the old test that asserted the refusal for one verb.
  - VTA `messaging::router::envelope_only_carriage` walks `dispatched_uris()` through `router::dispatch`.
- **Test harness**: `TestJoinClient::try_request`/`request` now send in the envelope. `try_request_task_typed` sends the forbidden shape, for the negative test only. Replies are classified by the document's type when they arrive in the envelope. New `test_support::served_trust_task_uris()`.
- **Docs**: `docs/03-vtc/credential-delivery.md` no longer says the VTC accepts task-typed submits. `vetting.md` says "in the binding envelope". `vtc-mvp.md`'s "DIDComm `type` is the Trust Task URL" is marked superseded.

## Breaking: migration for task-typed senders

A sender that puts the task URI in the DIDComm `type` for any VTC verb now gets a problem-report instead of an answer. To migrate, send the same document as the body of a DIDComm message whose `type` is `https://trusttasks.org/binding/didcomm/0.1/envelope`. This is what `vta_sdk::VtaClient::dispatch_trust_task`, `trust-tasks-didcomm` and the browser plugin already do. The self-remove and vmc bodies must be Trust Task documents (`payload` = the old body). The old bare bodies are no longer accepted.

**Known out-of-repo senders that break** (OpenVTC, `origin/main` 5453239):
- `openvtc-core/src/vetting/wire.rs::to_message` sends `join-requests/manifest/0.2`, `vtc/vetting/vetters/{list,profile,resend}/0.1` and `vtc/vetting/revoke-statement/0.1` **typed as the task** through `send_message` (DIDComm only). After this PR those get the problem-report, and `message_dispatch` surfaces it as "community refused something we sent". It needs to wrap in `TRUST_TASK_ENVELOPE_TYPE` the way `join.rs` and `members.rs` already do.
- `openvtc-core/src/personhood.rs::Route::send` sends `members/personhood/*` typed as the task. That was already refused before this PR, since there was never an arm for it. Only the comment changes.

OpenVTC's submit, status, self-remove, vmc and capability sends are already enveloped and are unaffected.

## Deliberately not in this PR

- **Reply `type` = envelope (binding §5).** `tt_didcomm_reply` still replies with the document's own `type`. OpenVTC keys VTC replies on `message.typ == JOIN_REQUEST_SUBMIT_RESPONSE_TYPE` and similar, and `vetting::wire::open` requires `document.type == message.typ`. Its envelope branch reads only capability replies. Switching would silently drop join verdicts and vetting answers. The opposite dependency also exists: `vta_sdk`'s DIDComm `dispatch_trust_task` (and so `vtc-client` over a DIDComm session without a TSP leg) and the browser plugin's `vta/didcomm.ts` both **require** an envelope-typed reply. They already fail against a VTC today. This needs OpenVTC to read the envelope first; a comment on `tt_didcomm_reply` records why.
- **VTA legacy task-typed arms.** The VTA router still answers two served URIs typed as the task: `acl/swap-key/0.1` (it shares a handler with FPN `swap-acl`) and `provision/integration/0.3` (still *sent* task-typed by `vta_sdk::provision_integration::didcomm`). They are pinned in `LEGACY_TASK_TYPED_ARMS`, which may only shrink.

## Tests

- `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vtc-client --no-fail-fast`
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --features tsp,didcomm-harness --test didcomm_envelope_binding --test join_didcomm`
- `cargo test -p vta-service --lib`: 1214 passed, 0 failed before a time limit on a heavily loaded box (load average about 12). The tests still running at the cutoff (`restore::…`, `routes::self_hosted_did::…`) pass when run alone. `trust_tasks::audit_coverage` takes about 20s per URI **with this PR's VTA changes stashed as well**, so the slowness is environmental and not caused by this change. `messaging::` (133 tests, including the new parity test) is green
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --all -- --check`

## Pre-merge checklist (stack dev guide §9)

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): no clients touched
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): none added
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1): the removed bespoke handlers were the paths that bypassed the spine; the remaining path is the spine's
- [x] Every retry is bounded and backed off (R1.4): no retries added
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): unchanged
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): unchanged
- [x] New/changed wire types (R3.*): no type changes. The carriage change is breaking and marked `!`. In-repo senders and the harness are migrated, and out-of-repo consumers (openvtc, pnm-browser-plugin, vti-didcomm-js, rp-sdk-js, cierge) were audited on `origin/main`, with the breakage listed above
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*): n/a
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.*): the refusal log says "refused", and the enveloped-refusal log reads the code from the error document
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): no mutations added
- [x] Deviations flagged: binding §5 (reply in the envelope) is not yet met; see "Deliberately not in this PR"

title: fix(vtc)!: a Trust Task over DIDComm rides the binding envelope only (Keyring VTI-42) (#1687)
body:
fix(vtc)!: a Trust Task over DIDComm rides the binding envelope only (Keyring VTI-42) (#1687)

The DIDComm binding (bindings/didcomm/0.2 §2-§5) makes the envelope
https://trusttasks.org/binding/didcomm/0.1/envelope the only carriage for a
Trust Task, and requires a consumer to refuse any other type at the DIDComm
layer with no trust-task-error.

The VTC router still carried twelve task-typed arms beside the envelope arm
(join-requests submit/manifest 0.1+0.2/status, members/self-remove,
members/vmc, six vtc/vetting URIs). Every other served verb answered
'unsupported message type' when typed as itself. Two of the arms
(self-remove, vmc) parsed bespoke bodies and bypassed
dispatch_trust_task_core, so they skipped freshness, recipient and proof
checks. All twelve are removed. Every one of these URIs is dispatched by the
spine via the envelope.

The VTC and VTA fallbacks now answer a https://trusttasks.org/spec/ type
with a threaded problem-report that names the envelope type.

Parity tests walk each dispatcher's own list (VTC DISPATCHED_URIS +
ROOMS_DISPATCHED_URIS; VTA dispatched_uris()). An enveloped request is never
answered 'unsupported message type'. A task-typed one gets the
envelope-naming problem-report. The VTA's two remaining task-typed arms
(acl/swap-key/0.1, provision/integration/0.3) are pinned in a shrink-only
list.

BREAKING: a sender that sets the DIDComm type to the task URI must move the
document into the binding envelope. Replies keep the document's own type for
now; see tt_didcomm_reply.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: docs(vtc): how the admin console comes to hold a signing key
body:
Refs #1641. Tracked by #1684. Design note only — no code.

#1681 moved the first four admin member verbs onto the signed-document dispatcher and could not retire their bearer routes, because the admin console cannot author a signed document. `vtc-trust-task-proof-enforcement.md` §6b states that as the removal point for **every** bearer route in the migration, so it is the thing standing between #1641 and closing. This note is how the console gets there.

## The premise, checked rather than assumed

`vtc-service/admin-ui/src` has no signing primitive of any kind — `eddsa-jcs-2022`, `DataIntegrityProof`, `ed25519`, `nacl`, `crypto.subtle`, `jcs`, `@noble`, `@scure`, `indexeddb` all return nothing outside `src/lib/wire.ts`, and those are generated OpenAPI comments. `package.json` carries no crypto dependency.

And the passkey route is **closed, not unexplored**: `docs/05-design-notes/webauthn-vti-v1-cryptosuite.md` — a cryptosuite that would have let a WebAuthn assertion *be* a Data-Integrity proof — was superseded in this repo on 2026-05-20, in favour of assertions travelling as payload data. Reopening it is a larger decision than this note.

## Three facts that shape the answer, none visible from the console

- **The operator already is a DID, with real key material they never use.** `vtc setup` takes the admin DID from the provisioning VTA and *prints its private key as JSON for the human to save by hand* (`setup/wizard.rs:277`, and the comment there says a keyring write is not yet implemented). The passkey is an authenticator attached to that DID string; the JWT `sub`, the audit actor and the ACL key are all that string. The browser has simply never held the key.
- **That DID is a `did:key`, which cannot grow a second verification method.** This is the entire reason a delegation is needed. §7 records that if the admin identity were a `did:webvh`, the console key would be published as a VM in the operator's own DID document and **not one line of VTC code would change**.
- **#1658's `Invariant::SelfPromotion` (VTI-OPS-050) blocks the obvious design.** Giving a console key its own admin ACL row is self-promotion reached by a longer path; `create_acl` already refuses a self-targeted new admin entry. Every new browser profile would need a second human.

## What it recommends

**A console signing key is a credential of the operator's existing admin DID, the way a passkey is** — not an identity of its own. A non-extractable Ed25519 `CryptoKey` in IndexedDB; the VTC stores a delegation ("key K may act as admin DID D") enrolled behind the step-up the console already runs, listed beside the passkeys, individually revocable, conferring no role on its own.

That sidesteps VTI-OPS-050 — a delegation confers no role, it names a credential of an identity that already holds one — and keeps #1681's stated property: authority is still an ACL row resolved at execution time, and `admin_signer` still never consults `sessions_ks`. It also reuses the multiplicity the VTC *does* model (one DID, many devices) rather than the one it does not (one human, many DIDs).

The cheaper alternative is set out honestly rather than dismissed: `vti_common::auth::session::Session` already carries `session_pubkey_b58btc`, documented for exactly this, plumbed through challenge/authenticate/refresh, and set to `None` by every console login. Taking it costs much less and gives up the property above.

## What it also does

- **States the exact construction** a browser must reproduce — `SHA-256(JCS(proofConfig)) || SHA-256(JCS(doc minus proof))`, signed over the 64 bytes, `z` + base58btc — with the three details that each yield a signature verifying nowhere: proof-config hash first, `proof` *removed* not nulled, and `created` never in the verifier's future (no skew tolerance; both existing browser implementations back-date, one of them after finding out).
- **Reads the two working browser implementations** and says which parts to take. `pnm-browser-plugin`'s `sign.ts` + `canonical.ts` are ~210 lines, browser-generic and ~15 KB gzip — but its key custody is a **plaintext extractable seed in IndexedDB by default**, which is an extension's posture, not a web origin's. `did-hosting-ui`'s `session-key.ts` is the closer precedent and already uses a `CryptoKey`.
- **Reports a key-custody bug in the closer precedent.** `session-key.ts` passes `extractable: true` to `generateKey`, on the stated reasoning that it is needed to export the raw public key. It is not: WebCrypto sets `publicKey.[[extractable]]` unconditionally and `privateKey.[[extractable]]` from the argument. Measured on Node 26 with a table — `extractable: false` still exports the 32-byte public key, and `true` makes `exportKey("pkcs8", privateKey)` succeed. Follow-up filed on #1684.
- **Rejects server-side signing explicitly**, as asked, rather than leaving it as an open option. VTI-OPS-021 says a transport that authenticates its sender does not relieve a producer of signing; a server signing for a cookie-bearing caller is that sentence with an extra hop, and every route it "unblocked" would be the same divergence wearing a signature. Also VTI-OPS-093, and it manufactures one compromise that forges the whole operator population.
- **Counts what it unblocks.** Re-derived from the console's own Type URIs against #1641's census: **34 of the 49**, including all four #1681 kept. The remainder are screens the console does not have (`config/{export,import}`, `backup/{export,import}`, `website/*`, `config/restart`) and member-session verbs belonging to clients that already sign.
- **Says what an XSS in the console origin gets** — the same bound as today, worse in one way (a signature is a durable replayable artefact within the 10-minute window) and better than the ACL-row design in another (it cannot leave anything behind).

## Scope

No code. The build is substantial — a keyspace, an enrolment verb pair that needs an upstream Trust Task spec first, an `admin_signer` change, a client module and a UI — and **four decisions in §8 belong to the operator**: A vs B, the browser-support floor, whether an operator may sign from two devices, and the default delegation lifetime. Those are in #1684.

## Files

- `docs/05-design-notes/vtc-console-signing.md` (new)
- `docs/README.md` — indexed beside the note it succeeds
- `docs/05-design-notes/vtc-trust-task-proof-enforcement.md` — one line in §6's step 4 pointing at it, where the removal point is stated

Deliberately **not** touched: `vtc-service/src/routes/`, the dispatcher, `admin-ui/openapi.json`, `src/lib/wire.ts`, `vtc/invitations/*` and `vti_common::auth` — all owned by other in-flight changes. The §6b batch record was left alone for the same reason.

title: feat(console): Mediator Lens — the relay carrying an agent's mail, seen from inside
body:
## Mediator Lens: the relay carrying an agent's mail, seen from inside

A mediator serves its own operations surface (`messaging/*`: statistics, every account's queues, one account's messages, a live traffic monitor) as Trust Tasks addressed to **its own DID**. The wallet already holds an authenticated session with it for each agent's inbox, so the console runs those tasks over that session, as that agent's holder. There is no new socket, no second CORS allowance and no key export. The terminal equivalent, `pnm messaging console`, has to export the DID's keys.

- **core**: `@openvtc/pnm-core/mediator` is subpath-only, like `admin` and `rooms`. It holds the typed helpers, `standingOf`, `accountHash`, one version floor (0.28.36), a monitor sequencer, and a preview-then-confirm purge that refuses a stale plan.
- **core**: `MediatorConnection.onMediatorFrame` keeps mediator-originated frames (monitor batches) off the persist-before-ack path. `DidcommVtaTransport` turns a problem report threaded by `pthid` into a coded `VtaClientError`.
- **extension**: `RUNTIME_MEDIATOR` accepts extension-page senders only, and the offscreen document re-checks the sender. The offscreen document only looks through a relay the wallet already uses (`mayOperateMediator`), runs a task allow-list (no `config/patch`, no `message/get`), and owns a 60 s monitor lease per console port.
- **console**: a Mediator pane in the Wire act. Transports gets "Look inside this relay", and DID detail gets "Where does its mail go?". A `standard` account is shown the exact `pnm messaging grant` command.
- **guards**: `messaging/*` is refused to pages. A fourth CI bundle guard permits exactly `manager.js` and the offscreen entry, with presence checks for both.

### Verified against a real mediator
A Node harness drives this package's own `pnm-core` against `affinidi-messaging-mediator` 0.29.x (the TDK test mediator, `trust_task_verification = enforce`):
- **24/24** checks pass: signed replies and monitor batches verify against the mediator's DID; replies are acked, so the receive queue stays at 0; a refusal arrives coded (`authorization.admin_required`) in 14 ms; monitor batches never reach `onInbound`; a grant takes effect.
- **On `vti-didcomm-js` 0.10.1, 6 of those checks fail**: 7 replies left in the queue, an 8 s timeout instead of a refusal, and monitor batches in the persist path. That is why `^0.11.0` is a correctness floor.

### Depends on
- **`@openvtc/vti-didcomm-js` 0.11.0** (OpenVTC/vti-didcomm-js#26, merged; **awaiting npm publish**). The lockfile is updated once it's on npm, and CI's `npm ci` fails until then.
- `@openvtc/trust-tasks` ^0.20.1 (published).
- affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#888: a role change now reaches a live socket. Without it, a fresh grant waits up to one token lifetime (15 min) to apply.
- OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1686: `pnm messaging grant`.

### Checklist
- [x] core 692 tests, extension 809 tests, all CI bundle guards run locally
- [x] rendered pane tests (standard vs admin vs too-old mediator vs no relay)
- [x] independent review pass; its six findings are fixed in the last commit
- [x] CLAUDE.md section "The Mediator Lens"

title: feat(pnm): messaging grant — give a DID an account role at a mediator
body:
A browser wallet's Mediator Lens looks inside the relay carrying its mail
as the wallet's holder did:key, and sees the whole mediator only once that
account is an admin there. Until now the only way to promote it was a
keypress in the interactive console. 'pnm messaging grant <DID> --role
admin' does it from a command the wallet can print exactly.

Acts as a context DID (or --as-session) exactly as 'messaging console'
does, refuses up front when that DID is not a mediator administrator, and
reports the role the mediator recorded rather than the one asked for,
failing when they differ. rootAdmin is not offered.

title: fix(forge): address the PR #62 review follow-ups
body:
fix(forge): address the PR #62 review follow-ups

Must-fix:
- F1: bodyless POST/PUT/PATCH now send `Content-Length: 0` (hyper sends
  no length for an empty body; GitHub answers 411). Covers the manifest
  conversion and the personal-account collaborator PUT; both tests assert
  the header.
- F2: `locate` and `bootstrap_plan` require exactly `host/owner/repo`
  (`Resource::require_owner_repo`), so a deserialised
  `github.com/acme/evil/widgets` is refused before any request instead of
  acting on `acme/widgets`.
- F4: a managed ruleset with any `exclude` pattern no longer counts as
  covering the default branch, so `refs/heads/*` is drift and the ruleset
  step re-applies.
- F5: token-request mocks match the body exactly, so an extra permission
  or repository fails the test. New tests cover the `/apps/github-actions`
  id lookup and a personal-account listing that includes the owner.
- F7: the manifest conversion requires `permissions`, `events` and
  `owner`; refuses an owner other than the one the admin intended (new
  `expected_owner` parameter), an events set other than the reviewed one,
  and `public: true`.

Also:
- F8: the personal-account owner is excluded from observed collaborators
  too, so it is never reported as drift or removed.
- F10: the App subscribes to `organization`; `membership` (team) maps to a
  new `TeamMembershipChanged`, `organization` to `OrgMembershipChanged`.
- F11: a directory at a bootstrap path, or a file too large for GitHub to
  return inline (`encoding: none`), is refused rather than overwritten.
- F12: `LinkStep`/`LinkCallback` Debug redact the device code; the member's
  user token is revoked after `/user` when the client secret is supplied
  (`with_client_secret`); polling is capped at the 15-minute device-code
  lifetime whatever `expires_in` the caller passes.
- F13: the workflow also runs on `merge_group`, with the queue's base sha
  as the range base.
- F14: `JwtIssuer::AppId` / `with_app_id_issuer()` for GHES.

F3 and F6 stay on the design track; F6 is recorded as an accepted
residual at the create_repo token site.

title: fix(lens): review findings — purge binds the shown plan; leases cannot leak
body:
fix(lens): review findings — purge binds the shown plan; leases cannot leak

- A purge confirmed the count the person read only in name: commit
  re-previewed, so the stale check compared two fresh counts and passed,
  removing whatever arrived meanwhile. The previewed plan is now kept and
  committed.
- A console closed during the session handshake left a monitor lease
  renewing forever: the disconnect listener is registered at connect,
  and a failed post stops the feed.
- The console treats a feed quiet past two heartbeats as ended — the
  service worker also holds the port, so a dead offscreen document does
  not close it.
- OFFSCREEN_MEDIATOR re-checks sender.url: a content script reaches the
  offscreen listener directly.
- A problem report with no sender is not accepted as a refusal.
- messaging/account/get joins the CI ban list; the grant command admits
  only DID-syntax characters.

title: refactor(verify-trust): take the resource grammar from vgi-core
body:
refactor(verify-trust): take the resource grammar from vgi-core

`normalize_qualified` now delegates to `vgi_core::normalize_resource`,
the grammar the VTC's registry projection and the forge adapters use, so
the resource a run queries is byte-for-byte the one a grant was written
under. verify-trust keeps what is its own: the flag name in messages
(`ResourceError::describe(what)`) and the forge host suggested from the
CI environment for an unqualified value.

One tightening, deliberate: path segments are now limited to ASCII
letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-` — every character GitHub, Forgejo and
GitLab allow in owner and repo names — so a value no forge could have
produced is refused rather than queried. `github..com/acme` now reports
an invalid forge host rather than a missing one.

title: vta-service-v0.40.0
body:
### Added

- **vta**: Advertise TSP on a minted DID when the mediator carries it ([#1665](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1665))

A persona minted by a TSP-capable VTA advertised only `DIDCommMessaging`,
  so a Rev 3 peer reading its document kept the leg on DIDComm (Keyring
  VTI-Q11). The cause: `addTspService` defaulted to `false` at the mint, and a
  persona is minted by a caller that sends no such field — the SDK skips it
  when false — so the answer was always "no" however TSP-capable the stack was.

  `addTspService` becomes three-state. An explicit `true` or `false` is
  honoured exactly as before. Absent now means "decide from what this VTA and
  its mediator can actually carry": `services.tsp` on, a mediator configured,
  and that mediator's own document advertising `TSPTransport` — the same check
  VTA setup makes before advertising `#tsp` for the VTA itself.

  A mediator that does not resolve answers no, which is deliberately stricter
  than setup's warn-and-proceed. There the operator named the mediator and is
  told; here nobody asked for `#tsp` at all, so the quiet default must not
  publish a transport peers cannot reach.

  Every internal caller passes `Some(false)`, so no existing path changes.



### Fixed

- **vta-service**: Answer a TSP relationship request before its sender's later traffic ([#1675](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1675))

Keyring VTI-43. A phone sent a TSP relationship invite (XRFI) and, 16 ms
  later, a Trust Task. The VTA's inbound loop reads frames in order but spawns
  each onto its own task, so the two raced: the task's ~2 ms reply (a
  permissionDenied) was sent ~328 ms before the VTA finished answering the
  invite with XRFA (accept_relationship resolves the peer VID and POSTs; only
  then is the relationship Bidirectional). The phone admits application
  messages only on a bidirectional relationship, so it dropped the reply. When
  the accept happened to win, it worked.

  The fix orders inbound frames per authenticated sender, taken on the reader
  task (the only place that sees arrival order) before spawning:

  - a TSP relationship-control frame is a barrier: it runs after every earlier
    barrier from the same sender;
  - TSP application frames run after every earlier barrier from their sender,
    but not after each other, and a barrier does not wait for earlier
    application frames — so a Trust Task awaiting a later message from the same
    peer (a step-up approval) cannot deadlock on it, which a per-sender FIFO
    would;
  - different senders never wait for each other; DIDComm stays unordered.

  The bookkeeping map holds only senders with a barrier in flight (bounded by
  the loop's concurrency cap) and a wait is bounded at 15 s (R1.3): a hung
  accept degrades the frames behind it to the old unordered behaviour rather
  than stranding the peer. A barrier's handler releases its followers on drop,
  so a failure or panic releases them too.

  vtc-service needs no change: its inbound loop awaits each frame inline, so
  it already processes one sender's frames in arrival order.



### Security

- **persona**: The correlation answer on a local write is the holder's ([#1676](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1676))

Two defects in one task, found while writing a test for the first.

  **The oracle.** `persona/local/profile/put` is context-scoped, and its
  response carried `correlation.matchesPoolValue` — a yes/no on "does the
  holder hold this exact value anywhere", computed from the agent-wide
  index. A caller that can write is a caller that can guess, so any
  application authorized in one context had an unbounded oracle over the
  whole pool: one guess per write, each answer confirming or eliminating
  one. No value crosses the boundary and none needs to — for a name, an
  address or a date of birth, confirmation is disclosure.

  The member is now told only to a caller that passes the holder test, and
  omitted rather than softened: a coarser signal is still an oracle, only a
  slower one. The holder still learns it, through the audit row (which
  records it whoever asked) and `persona/correlation/analyze`. Conditional
  by the specification too, as of dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#609.

  **The unsendable payload.** Writing that test showed the agent refusing
  its own SDK's request: `LocalProfileEntry` reused the pool's
  `InlineValue`, whose `provenance` is required, and the schema has no such
  member for a context-local entry and sets `additionalProperties: false`.
  So every local-profile write this SDK could build was rejected —
  `persona_local_profile_put` could not express a conforming payload at
  all. `LocalInlineValue` is that type without the member, which is the
  boundary rather than an omission: a credentialBacked provenance names a
  credentialId and a claimPath, and a context has nowhere to put either.

  The rule against hand-writing a payload type for a task that has a
  generated module exists for exactly this; the generated type never had
  the member.

- **persona**: Holder authority is granted, never inherited from a role ([#1673](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1673))

`persona-holder` exists because no role carries authority over the
  holder's pool — and super-admin carried it anyway. That left the premise
  true only of the roles nobody automates with: the unrestricted admin
  credential is the one most likely to be sitting in a script, and it read
  the attribute pool, the faces over it and the disclosure history without
  an ACL entry saying so.

  Now the grant is the only way in. A super-admin can still grant itself
  the capability, so this is not a boundary it cannot cross; it is the
  difference between crossing it and crossing it deliberately. The grant is
  an ACL write — audited, reviewable, revocable on its own — where the
  inherited form left no trace that the pool had been read by something
  that never asked for it.

  The refusal names the command that fixes it, because an operator refused
  against their own agent's own pool cannot guess at a capability they have
  never heard of.

  Operators upgrading: `pnm acl update --did <did> --capabilities
  persona-holder`, or `pnm contexts create --admin-holder` when
  provisioning a client that is the holder's own.

  §7 of the persona design note records this and the three other questions
  it left open, with the reasoning rather than only the outcome.

title: feat(forge): add vgi-forge and the GitHub adapter
body:
feat(forge): add vgi-forge and the GitHub adapter

vgi-forge is the forge-neutral seam for VTC-governed git namespaces: the
object-safe `Forge` trait (async-trait, so a bridge can hold one
`Box<dyn Forge>` per forge host), `ForgeHooks` returning
Continue / Modify(plan) / Abort(reason), `Capabilities`, `Resource` on the
vgi-core grammar, `EffectiveRights` with own ⇒ maintain ⇒ commit, role
projection that rounds down onto a forge's ladder, check-then-apply
bootstrap plans with `run_plan`, `ForgeEvent` and `Drift`.

vgi-forge-github implements it as one community's own GitHub App:
manifest registration with a fixed permission set, RS256 App JWTs through
an `AppKeySigner` (enclave-ready), per-operation installation tokens
scoped to one repo and that operation's permissions, state-checked
namespace binding, device-flow account linking, repo create / inspect /
archive, role convergence keyed on numeric ids, the §5.3 bootstrap
(pinned workflow, web-flow keyring, variables, a ruleset with no bypass
actors and the check pinned to the Actions App), and constant-time
verified webhooks. A personal account is the same adapter reporting a
reduced capability set.

HTTP is a thin reqwest client rather than octocrab (unscoped, cached
installation tokens; in-memory JWT key; no variables API; follows
redirects). No package is added to the normal dependency graph.

title: feat(vgi-core): add the forge-qualified resource grammar
body:
feat(vgi-core): add the forge-qualified resource grammar

`normalize_resource` / `normalize_resource_with_depth` turn
`GitHub.com/Acme/Widgets` into `github.com/acme/widgets` and refuse
everything else that is not canonical — the legacy `owner/repo` form, a
URL scheme, a port, empty or dot segments, odd characters — with a
message that says what to write instead. `resource_contains` is the
segment-prefix scope check (a namespace contains its repos, never
another owner's or another forge's).

It lives in vgi-core, dependency-free, so the verifier, the VTC's
registry projection and the forge adapters all produce the same bytes
for the same repository.

title: pnm-cli-v0.22.0
body:
### Added

- **cli**: Pnm reaches worlds and the claim-type registry ([#1663](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1663))

`persona/facet/{put,list,delete}` and `persona/claim-types/list` had no
  method on `VtaClient` at all, so `pnm` could not reach them even though
  both graphical clients do. The SDK gains the four, built from the
  generated specification types rather than hand-written bodies, and
  decoding their responses into the generated `Response` — a shape the
  specification does not describe is then an error at the call rather than
  a `None` three screens later.

  `pnm persona world {list,put,delete}` and `pnm persona claim-types`
  follow. Both id lists on a put replace: the specification is explicit
  that a member whose absence meant "keep" would make emptying a world
  impossible, so the CLI passes them through as given and says so.

  The colour is a ValueEnum whose mapping to the specification's tokens is
  written out rather than derived, pinned from both sides — `pnm-cli` does
  not depend on the generated types and `vta-cli-common` does not know the
  CLI's enum, so the pair of tests is what holds the wire value end to end.



### Security

- **persona**: Holder authority is granted, never inherited from a role ([#1673](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1673))

`persona-holder` exists because no role carries authority over the
  holder's pool — and super-admin carried it anyway. That left the premise
  true only of the roles nobody automates with: the unrestricted admin
  credential is the one most likely to be sitting in a script, and it read
  the attribute pool, the faces over it and the disclosure history without
  an ACL entry saying so.

  Now the grant is the only way in. A super-admin can still grant itself
  the capability, so this is not a boundary it cannot cross; it is the
  difference between crossing it and crossing it deliberately. The grant is
  an ACL write — audited, reviewable, revocable on its own — where the
  inherited form left no trace that the pool had been read by something
  that never asked for it.

  The refusal names the command that fixes it, because an operator refused
  against their own agent's own pool cannot guess at a capability they have
  never heard of.

  Operators upgrading: `pnm acl update --did <did> --capabilities
  persona-holder`, or `pnm contexts create --admin-holder` when
  provisioning a client that is the holder's own.

  §7 of the persona design note records this and the three other questions
  it left open, with the reasoning rather than only the outcome.

title: vtc-client-v0.7.3
body:
### Added

- **vtc**: A by-DID vetter status lookup ([#1671](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1671))

The vetter listing omits a vetter with no published profile and one whose
  grant was revoked in exactly the same way: both are simply absent. An
  applicant whose vetter went quiet could not tell which had happened, and a
  vetter could not check their own standing at all (Keyring VTI-Q3, #1651).

  `vtc/vetting/vetters/show/0.1` answers by DID with `live`, `revoked`,
  `expired` or `none`, the grant's id, the timestamp that ended or will end it,
  and — for a live grant — whether the vetter is listed. That last member is
  what separates "unlisted by choice" from "not a vetter".

  Served over `/v1/trust-tasks`, DIDComm and TSP for applicants and members,
  and as `POST /v1/vetting/vetters/show` for the console. `vtc-client` gains
  `show_vetter`.

  The live case goes through the same `live_grant` lookup the listing and every
  grant check use, so "live here" cannot drift from "live there". Where a grant
  is both revoked and expired the answer is `revoked`: the community
  withdrawing trust and a grant lapsing are different statements, and a vetter
  told `expired` would reasonably ask for a renewal.

  `CheckShape` on the response enforces what one object's schema cannot — which
  members belong to which status. A response saying `revoked` while carrying
  `validUntil` and no `revokedAt` reads as an expiry to a client branching on
  members rather than status.

  Requires trust-tasks-rs 0.21.21, which publishes the spec merged as
  trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#603.

title: vti-common-v0.23.1
body:
### Fixed

- **auth**: Consume the challenge before minting, atomically ([#1664](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1664))

`handle_authenticate` read the challenge row, checked it was in
  `ChallengeSent`, then looked up the ACL and minted tokens, and only after
  all that deleted the row. Those are awaits, and the row stayed alive across
  them, so two interleaved presentations of the same signed envelope both
  passed the state check and both minted. Sequentially it was correct; under
  concurrency the single-use challenge was not single-use ([#1656](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1656)).

  Sessions coalesce per DID (last write wins, access token pinned by
  `token_id`), so an attacker who captured a correctly-addressed envelope and
  replayed it inside the freshness window while the holder signed in could win
  the race, hold the session as the holder, and supersede the holder's own
  access token.

  follow. Both id lists on a put replace: the specification is explicit
  that a member whose absence meant "keep" would make emptying a world
  impossible, so the CLI passes them through as given and says so.

  written out rather than derived, pinned from both sides — `pnm-cli` does
  not depend on the generated types and `vta-cli-common` does not know the
  CLI's enum, so the pair of tests is what holds the wire value end to end.



### Fixed

- Use shared_tdk_config for unified DID resolution ([#1661](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1661))


### Security

- **persona**: The correlation answer on a local write is the holder's ([#1676](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1676))

Two defects in one task, found while writing a test for the first.

  **The oracle.** `persona/local/profile/put` is context-scoped, and its
  response carried `correlation.matchesPoolValue` — a yes/no on "does the
  holder hold this exact value anywhere", computed from the agent-wide
  index. A caller that can write is a caller that can guess, so any
  application authorized in one context had an unbounded oracle over the
  whole pool: one guess per write, each answer confirming or eliminating
  one. No value crosses the boundary and none needs to — for a name, an
  address or a date of birth, confirmation is disclosure.

  slower one. The holder still learns it, through the audit row (which
  records it whoever asked) and `persona/correlation/analyze`. Conditional

  its own SDK's request: `LocalProfileEntry` reused the pool's
  `InlineValue`, whose `provenance` is required, and the schema has no such
  member for a context-local entry and sets `additionalProperties: false`.

  `persona_local_profile_put` could not express a conforming payload at
  all. `LocalInlineValue` is that type without the member, which is the
  boundary rather than an omission: a credentialBacked provenance names a
  credentialId and a claimPath, and a context has nowhere to put either.

  generated module exists for exactly this; the generated type never had
  the member.

title: fix(action): install verify-trust without gh or a GitHub token
body:
fix(action): install verify-trust without gh or a GitHub token

The install step used `gh release download` with the job token and
RUNNER_OS/RUNNER_ARCH. On a Forgejo runner `gh` is usually absent, the
job token belongs to the Forgejo instance, and RUNNER_* may be unset,
so the action could not run there.

- Download the public release anonymously with curl (--fail --location
  --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2, retried); resolve `latest` from the
  releases/latest redirect; validate the tag before it goes in a URL.
- Detect the platform from RUNNER_OS/RUNNER_ARCH, else uname, and fail
  naming an unsupported platform.
- Integrity: the tarball must match the SHA-256 published with the
  release (as before - transport integrity only). New: when gh is
  present and the runner is on github.com, also verify the
  build-provenance attestation from release.yml for the tag
  (verify-attestation: auto|true|false). New `sha256` input pins a
  checksum in the caller's workflow for runners without attestation.
- The job token is bound as VGI_GITHUB_TOKEN and passed only to
  `gh attestation verify`, and only on github.com.
- action-selftest pins v0.4.12 (first attested release is v0.4.9) and
  adds a gh-less container job; ci_workflow_hardening gates curl flags,
  the absence of gh on the download path and of an exported token.
- README and RUNBOOK document Forgejo use and its integrity trade-off.

## [0.22.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/pnm-cli-v0.21.0...pnm-cli-v0.22.0) — 2026-09-23 ### Added - **cli**: Pnm reaches worlds and the claim-type registry ([#1663](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1663)) `persona/facet/{put,list,delete}` and `persona/claim-types/list` had no method on `VtaClient` at all, so `pnm` could not reach them even though both graphical clients do. The SDK gains the four, built from the generated specification types rather than hand-written bodies, and decoding their responses into the generated `Response` — a shape the specification does not describe is then an error at the call rather than a `None` three screens later. `pnm persona world {list,put,delete}` and `pnm persona claim-types` follow. Both id lists on a put replace: the specification is explicit that a member whose absence meant "keep" would make emptying a world impossible, so the CLI passes them through as given and says so. The colour is a ValueEnum whose mapping to the specification's tokens is written out rather than derived, pinned from both sides — `pnm-cli` does not depend on the generated types and `vta-cli-common` does not know the CLI's enum, so the pair of tests is what holds the wire value end to end. ### Security - **persona**: Holder authority is granted, never inherited from a role ([#1673](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1673)) `persona-holder` exists because no role carries authority over the holder's pool — and super-admin carried it anyway. That left the premise true only of the roles nobody automates with: the unrestricted admin credential is the one most likely to be sitting in a script, and it read the attribute pool, the faces over it and the disclosure history without an ACL entry saying so. Now the grant is the only way in. A super-admin can still grant itself the capability, so this is not a boundary it cannot cross; it is the difference between crossing it and crossing it deliberately. The grant is an ACL write — audited, reviewable, revocable on its own — where the inherited form left no trace that the pool had been read by something that never asked for it. The refusal names the command that fixes it, because an operator refused against their own agent's own pool cannot guess at a capability they have never heard of. Operators upgrading: `pnm acl update --did --capabilities persona-holder`, or `pnm contexts create --admin-holder` when provisioning a client that is the holder's own. §7 of the persona design note records this and the three other questions it left open, with the reasoning rather than only the outcome.
## `vti-rooms-dtg`
## [0.3.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vti-rooms-dtg-v0.2.14...vti-rooms-dtg-v0.3.0) — 2026-09-23 ### Build & CI - **deps**: Dtg-credentials 0.11 ([#1669](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1669))
## `vta-service`
## [0.40.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-service-v0.39.0...vta-service-v0.40.0) — 2026-09-23 ### Added - **vta**: Advertise TSP on a minted DID when the mediator carries it ([#1665](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1665)) A persona minted by a TSP-capable VTA advertised only `DIDCommMessaging`, so a Rev 3 peer reading its document kept the leg on DIDComm (Keyring VTI-Q11). The cause: `addTspService` defaulted to `false` at the mint, and a persona is minted by a caller that sends no such field — the SDK skips it when false — so the answer was always "no" however TSP-capable the stack was. `addTspService` becomes three-state. An explicit `true` or `false` is honoured exactly as before. Absent now means "decide from what this VTA and its mediator can actually carry": `services.tsp` on, a mediator configured, and that mediator's own document advertising `TSPTransport` — the same check VTA setup makes before advertising `#tsp` for the VTA itself. A mediator that does not resolve answers no, which is deliberately stricter than setup's warn-and-proceed. There the operator named the mediator and is told; here nobody asked for `#tsp` at all, so the quiet default must not publish a transport peers cannot reach. Every internal caller passes `Some(false)`, so no existing path changes. ### Fixed - **vta-service**: Answer a TSP relationship request before its sender's later traffic ([#1675](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1675)) Keyring VTI-43. A phone sent a TSP relationship invite (XRFI) and, 16 ms later, a Trust Task. The VTA's inbound loop reads frames in order but spawns each onto its own task, so the two raced: the task's ~2 ms reply (a permissionDenied) was sent ~328 ms before the VTA finished answering the invite with XRFA (accept_relationship resolves the peer VID and POSTs; only then is the relationship Bidirectional). The phone admits application messages only on a bidirectional relationship, so it dropped the reply. When the accept happened to win, it worked. The fix orders inbound frames per authenticated sender, taken on the reader task (the only place that sees arrival order) before spawning: - a TSP relationship-control frame is a barrier: it runs after every earlier barrier from the same sender; - TSP application frames run after every earlier barrier from their sender, but not after each other, and a barrier does not wait for earlier application frames — so a Trust Task awaiting a later message from the same peer (a step-up approval) cannot deadlock on it, which a per-sender FIFO would; - different senders never wait for each other; DIDComm stays unordered. The bookkeeping map holds only senders with a barrier in flight (bounded by the loop's concurrency cap) and a wait is bounded at 15 s (R1.3): a hung accept degrades the frames behind it to the old unordered behaviour rather than stranding the peer. A barrier's handler releases its followers on drop, so a failure or panic releases them too. vtc-service needs no change: its inbound loop awaits each frame inline, so it already processes one sender's frames in arrival order. ### Security - **persona**: The correlation answer on a local write is the holder's ([#1676](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1676)) Two defects in one task, found while writing a test for the first. **The oracle.** `persona/local/profile/put` is context-scoped, and its response carried `correlation.matchesPoolValue` — a yes/no on "does the holder hold this exact value anywhere", computed from the agent-wide index. A caller that can write is a caller that can guess, so any application authorized in one context had an unbounded oracle over the whole pool: one guess per write, each answer confirming or eliminating one. No value crosses the boundary and none needs to — for a name, an address or a date of birth, confirmation is disclosure. The member is now told only to a caller that passes the holder test, and omitted rather than softened: a coarser signal is still an oracle, only a slower one. The holder still learns it, through the audit row (which records it whoever asked) and `persona/correlation/analyze`. Conditional by the specification too, as of dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#609. **The unsendable payload.** Writing that test showed the agent refusing its own SDK's request: `LocalProfileEntry` reused the pool's `InlineValue`, whose `provenance` is required, and the schema has no such member for a context-local entry and sets `additionalProperties: false`. So every local-profile write this SDK could build was rejected — `persona_local_profile_put` could not express a conforming payload at all. `LocalInlineValue` is that type without the member, which is the boundary rather than an omission: a credentialBacked provenance names a credentialId and a claimPath, and a context has nowhere to put either. The rule against hand-writing a payload type for a task that has a generated module exists for exactly this; the generated type never had the member. - **persona**: Holder authority is granted, never inherited from a role ([#1673](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1673)) `persona-holder` exists because no role carries authority over the holder's pool — and super-admin carried it anyway. That left the premise true only of the roles nobody automates with: the unrestricted admin credential is the one most likely to be sitting in a script, and it read the attribute pool, the faces over it and the disclosure history without an ACL entry saying so. Now the grant is the only way in. A super-admin can still grant itself the capability, so this is not a boundary it cannot cross; it is the difference between crossing it and crossing it deliberately. The grant is an ACL write — audited, reviewable, revocable on its own — where the inherited form left no trace that the pool had been read by something that never asked for it. The refusal names the command that fixes it, because an operator refused against their own agent's own pool cannot guess at a capability they have never heard of. Operators upgrading: `pnm acl update --did --capabilities persona-holder`, or `pnm contexts create --admin-holder` when provisioning a client that is the holder's own. §7 of the persona design note records this and the three other questions it left open, with the reasoning rather than only the outcome.

title: feat(console): Mediator Lens — the relay carrying an agent's mail, seen from inside
body:
feat(console): Mediator Lens — the relay carrying an agent's mail, seen from inside

A mediator serves its own operations surface (messaging/*: statistics,
every account's queues, one account's messages, a live traffic monitor)
as Trust Tasks addressed to its own DID. The wallet already holds an
authenticated session with it for each agent's inbox, so the console can
run those tasks over that session as the agent's holder: no new socket,
no second CORS allowance, no key export.

- core: @openvtc/pnm-core/mediator (subpath-only) — typed helpers,
  standingOf, accountHash, a single version floor (0.28.36), a monitor
  sequencer, and a preview-then-confirm purge that refuses a stale plan.
- core: MediatorConnection.onMediatorFrame keeps mediator-originated
  frames (monitor batches) off the persist-before-ack inbound path, and
  DidcommVtaTransport turns a pthid-threaded problem report into a coded
  VtaClientError instead of a parse error or a timeout.
- extension: RUNTIME_MEDIATOR relay (extension-page senders only), an
  offscreen channel that only looks through a relay the wallet already
  uses and runs an allow-list of tasks (no config/patch, no message/get),
  and a per-port monitor lease owned by the offscreen document.
- console: a Mediator pane in the Wire act; 'Look inside this relay'
  from Transports, 'Where does its mail go?' from a DID.
- guards: messaging/* refused to pages; a fourth CI bundle guard with
  manager.js and the offscreen entry as the only permitted files.

vti-didcomm-js ^0.11.0 is a correctness floor: below it replies pile up
in the holder's receive queue, refusals time out, and monitor batches
reach onInbound — all three reproduced against a real mediator.

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.22.2
body:
### Added

- **vtc/vetting/vetters/event-mode**: The exception to the constant drip ([#620](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/620))

A vetter's ordinary rate is a few tokens a tick, whether or not they have
  vetted anyone. That is the right rate for ordinary weeks and the wrong one for
  a conference desk, and the answer is deliberately not a bigger drip under the
  same key: it is a separate token label for a named event, with its own rate,
  its own expiry, and a group of vetters large enough that a spend under it still
  hides one.

  This task carries the vetter's half of that, which is only ever a request. The
  approval is an act by someone else, through the community's own administrative
  surface, and the specification says why there is no Trust Task for it: a task
  the vetter could send is a task a vetter could be made to send.

  The response says where the request stands, and carries a group *count* rather
  than a group. Who else is at the event is the anonymity set, so the number is
  the most a member may be told — enough to tell "nobody has approved it" from
  "not enough people have asked", which are the two reasons a request waits.

- **vetting/attestation**: The four tasks hidden-vetter admission needs ([#618](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/618))

* feat(vetting/attestation): the four tasks hidden-vetter admission needs

  A community can hide which of its vetters vetted an applicant: the vetter
  attests under a blind class credential, the applicant proves that k distinct
  holders of one attested it, and the community counts the proof with the rule
  it already counts named statements with. What was missing was the wire.

  Four specifications, and the split between them is the design:

  - vtc/vetting/vetters/pcs-root — a vetter enrols for a class label. The
    community checks its own records (a live vetter grant, no credential under
    this label yet, the identifier it was bound to) and signs a commitment it
    cannot open. Being named happens here, once per label, and nowhere else on
    the path.
  - vtc/vetting/vetters/pcs-tokens — the vetter draws its tick of attestation
    tokens, unconditionally and at a published rate. A draw that tracked demand
    would report activity, which is what the exchange exists to hide; the quota
    is the community's to enforce, never the asker's restraint.
  - vetting/attestation — vetter to applicant, carrying the facts of the session
    and no issuer. The delivering identity is deliberately NOT what makes it
    count, and a consumer is told not to record it beside the attestation: that
    would recreate, in the applicant's own store, the link the exchange removes.
  - vtc/vetting/pcs-challenge — the applicant asks the community for the
    single-use nonce its proof must bind. Without it a proof verifies as often
    as it is submitted, and the second submission counts as readily as the first.

  vetting/attestation declares identifierScope: any. Nothing in it needs a
  reusable identifier — the community never sees the document, and the applicant
  only needs the identifier the session was held under — so a pair that runs the
  whole vetting exchange pairwise loses nothing.

  Bindings regenerated for all four languages; conformance checks agree.

title: feat(vtc/vetting/vetters/event-mode): the exception to the constant drip
body:
A fifth specification for hidden-vetter admission, following the four merged in #618.

A vetter's ordinary rate is a few attestation tokens a tick, drawn whether or not they have
vetted anyone. That is the right rate for ordinary weeks and the wrong one for a conference desk,
where one member may sit down and meet twenty people in a day.

Event mode is the exception, and it is deliberately **not** a bigger drip. It is a separate token
label for a named event, with its own rate, its own expiry, and a group of vetters that must be
large enough before the label exists at all. This task is how a vetter asks to be in that group.

### Three things it is not

**Not self-service.** The vetter asks; someone else approves. Raising your own cap is exactly what
a coerced vetter would be made to do, so the request and the grant are separate acts by separate
parties, and this task carries only the first. There is deliberately no Trust Task for the
approval — a task the vetter could send is a task a vetter could be made to send — and the
Authorization section says so, which is where a future implementer will look for permission to
add the convenience.

**Not a bigger number under the same key.** Tokens live and die with their label. Three days at
twenty a day under the monthly key would leave sixty tokens spendable for the rest of the month;
under an event key they expire shortly after the event, which is what bounds the stockpile.

**Not free.** A spend under an event label narrows the anonymity set from *some vetter in this
community* to *some vetter at this event*. That is why the group floor exists, and why the
specification says an `eventId` names a gathering rather than a desk. A consumer **MUST**
implement all three mitigations — the floor, the expiry, and the naming — rather than picking
among them: a community that approves a two-person event with a floor of three has published a
coin flip.

### The response carries a count, never a group

`groupSize` and `groupFloor` exist so that a vetter waiting on an event can tell the two reasons
for waiting apart: nobody has approved it yet, or not enough people have asked. Who *else* is at
the event is the anonymity set itself, so a count is the most a member may be told.

### Mechanics

- Bindings regenerated for all four languages; `npm run check-bindings` agrees (483 specs).
- Six declared error codes; the response is titled so the TypeScript binding exports a `Response`
  type; dates rather than timestamps on the window, for the same reason `vetting/attestation`
  carries dates.
- `payload.invalid-examples.json` is not included, matching the four in #618 — happy to add
  fixtures for the negative space if reviewers want them.

Implemented against this schema in both halves of a VTC deployment, including the four conditions
a consumer checks before serving a token under an event label.

title: spec(messaging/account): opt-in activity timestamps on account/get and account/list
body:
## What

Two optional members on the shared `Account` record, so an operator can see when each account was last active:

- `lastReceivedAt`: Unix epoch seconds when the mediator last accepted a message addressed to the account. It may lag by up to 60 seconds, so a mediator can throttle the write instead of adding one to every message.
- `lastAuthenticatedAt`: Unix epoch seconds when the account last completed authentication, over any transport.

Both use epoch seconds, like `AuditEntry.timestamp`.

## Why opt-in

`account/get` and `account/list` each gain an optional request member, `includeActivity`. A mediator returns the timestamps only when it is `true`, and **MUST NOT** otherwise.

The generated clients reject unknown members (`deny_unknown_fields` in Rust, `additionalProperties: false` in the schema). A mediator that always sent the new members would break every existing requester that parses these responses. With the flag, older requesters never see them.

In the other direction, a requester that sends `includeActivity` to an older mediator gets a schema rejection. The prose says a requester **SHOULD** set it only where it knows the mediator supports it.

The change is additive inside version 0.1 of `messaging/account/{get,list}`: every existing document stays valid.

## Also

- Security & Privacy notes for both tasks: these timestamps are a behavioural signal beyond the account's configuration, so they get the same authorization as the rest of the account view.
- All four client libraries regenerated (Rust, TS, Go, Dart). `npm run build`, `npm run check-bindings` and `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` pass.

title: feat(persona): derived provenance, and endorsements as inventory
body:
Design note (VTI docs/05-design-notes/persona-context-first.md) §5.7.

Provenance gains `derived` {source, derivedAt}: a value taken from a
source the holder connected or supplied — a code-hosting profile, an
uploaded CV — that the holder did not type and no issuer signed. It is
the holder's claim that the source said so, and a consumer must not
present it as attested. `source` names the KIND of source (`github`,
`cvUpload`), never a handle or URL: provenance reaches the verifier, and
a handle there would disclose an identifier the holder never chose to
share. For how strongly a disclosed value identifies the holder the
kinds rank credentialBacked > derived > selfAsserted. The preview's
provenance enum gains `derived`.

Attribute gains `endorsements`: vault ids of credentials in which a
third party endorses the value. Inventory, not evidence — a vouched
self-assertion is still self-asserted, and folding a vouch into
provenance would render it as attested. Not disclosed with the value.
attribute/put takes it and refuses an id the vault does not hold
(`endorsementNotFound`).

title: feat(rs): emit each specification's declared error codes
body:
## Why

A specification's `errorCodes` front matter (SPEC §7.3 item 9) never reached the Rust bindings. An implementation could only spell a declared extended code as a string literal. Nothing checked that the literal was a code the specification declares, or that the service emitted the declared codes at all.

That gap has already shipped a bug. Downstream, `vtc/join-requests/withdraw/0.1` answered both of its declared codes (`notFound`, `alreadyDecided`) as a bare `taskFailed`, and every gate stayed green. OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1600 has the details. The fix the downstream census needs is to derive the declared codes from the specifications, as it already does for Type URIs, rather than keep a list by hand. This PR provides that input.

## What the generated API looks like

Every generated module now carries:

```rust
/// The extended error codes this specification declares (SPEC §7.3 item 9,
/// §8.5), in declaration order. Empty when it declares none.
pub const ERROR_CODES: &[crate::DeclaredErrorCode] = &[error_codes::NOT_FOUND, error_codes::ALREADY_DECIDED];

pub mod error_codes {            // only when the spec declares any
    /// `vtc/join-requests/withdraw:notFound`
    ///
    /// <the declared `meaning`>
    ///
    /// Declared `retryable: false`.
    pub const NOT_FOUND: crate::DeclaredErrorCode = crate::DeclaredErrorCode {
        code: "vtc/join-requests/withdraw:notFound",
        retryable: false,
    };
    // ...
}
```

`schema_index` also gains a lookup by URI:

```rust
pub fn error_codes_for(type_uri: &str) -> Option<&'static [DeclaredErrorCode]>
```

It is keyed on the bare request Type URI. `Some(&[])` means the spec declares no codes and `None` means the URI is unknown. The two are different answers, so a census cannot pass a task it has never heard of. The function is feature-gated per family, like `schema_for`.

`DeclaredErrorCode` is a new `#[non_exhaustive]` type:
- `code: &'static str`, the fully qualified wire string. It works in a `const`: `const X: &str = withdraw::v0_1::error_codes::NOT_FOUND.code;`
- `retryable: bool`, as the spec declares it.
- `namespace()`, `local()` and `matches(&TrustTaskCode)`.
- An infallible `From<DeclaredErrorCode> for TrustTaskCode`.
- A `From<DeclaredErrorCode> for ErrorPayload` that uses the declared `retryable` rather than the §8.5 default.

It deliberately has no `PartialEq<DeclaredErrorCode> for TrustTaskCode`. A second `PartialEq` impl makes every existing `assert_eq!(code, StandardCode::X.into())` ambiguous, and the in-crate tests showed that directly.

Constants are named for the local part in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE. Frozen 0.1 snake_case locals (`role_not_recognized`) produce the same shape of name as lowerCamelCase ones. Family-namespace codes (`keys:notFound` on `keys/revoke`, §8.5 rule 2) keep their family namespace in `code`.

## Guards

- **The generator refuses bad declarations.** It fails on a code that does not parse, on a namespace that is neither the slug nor a path prefix of it, and on two declarations that would claim one constant (`notFound` vs `not_found`, or `keys:notFound` beside `keys/revoke:notFound`). None exist today, but the conversion to `TrustTaskCode` is infallible on the strength of this check.
- **`check-bindings` compares every Rust `ERROR_CODES` against front matter.** The expected lists are re-derived independently, like the policy constants. It resolves the slice through the `error_codes` constants, so a constant left out of the slice also counts as a disagreement. It currently reports `891 declared error codes match Rust ERROR_CODES`. I also checked by hand that a mutated generated code fails the check.
- **Tests.** There are codegen unit tests for parsing, naming, refusals and empty rendering. `trust-tasks-rs/tests/error_codes.rs` has consumer-view spot checks. The index half is gated on `validate`, because `schema_index` is.

## Other language bindings

This PR emits error codes for Rust only. TypeScript, Go and Dart each have their own generator, and CLAUDE.md asks that those generators stay independent. Emitting in all four is a follow-up. It would add the other three to the same `check-bindings` comparison so the four agree with each other, not only with the front matter. CLAUDE.md now has a section saying so, and the CI-check table mentions the new comparison.

## Release

The change is additive: new items, a new type and new `From` impls. I have not bumped any version or edited a changelog. The title is the changelog entry.

## Verified locally
- `cargo test --workspace --all-targets` and `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --all-features`: green.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` and trust-tasks-rs `--all-features`: clean.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: clean.
- `npm run check-bindings`: all agree.
- A downstream prototype of the census in VTI, against this branch through a `[patch.crates-io]` path, is described on #1600.

title: feat(spec): vtc/admin/did-log/install/0.1 — deliver a community its own did:webvh log
body:
Adds **`vtc/admin/did-log/install/0.1`**: a community administrator delivers the community its own `did:webvh` log, extended by entries the DID's key holder signed. The community verifies the log and serves it in place of the one it serves now.

## Why

This is for a community (VTC) that **self-hosts** its `did.jsonl`. A community whose DID is on a DID host doesn't need it: the agent holding the keys publishes each new entry to that host directly. A self-hosted community serves a log it can't extend, because the keys belong to the agent that provisioned it, which can't reach the community's copy. So any change to the community's DID document after mint (adding a TSP or DIDComm transport, rotating a key) produces a log entry the community can't make and has no way to receive. Operators have been copying the file onto the host by hand. This was reported by the Keyring team as VTI-35, and VTI-12 is the same shape for DIDComm.

## Shape

- **Request:** `log`, the complete JSON Lines log from the first entry. A delta is not conforming, because the consumer verifies the chain from its start.
- **Response:** `did`, `versionId`, `previousVersionId`, `entriesAdded`. Installing the log already served is idempotent and returns `entriesAdded: 0`.
- **Consumer rules**, all checked before anything is served:
  1. The whole log verifies (proofs under the update keys in force, SCID, entry-hash chain). Otherwise `invalidLog`.
  2. The log is for the community's own DID. Otherwise `wrongDid`.
  3. Every served entry appears unchanged and in order as a prefix. Otherwise `notAnExtension`, which catches a shorter, rewritten or forked log.
  4. The community self-hosts its log at all. Otherwise `notServedHere`, the did-hosting case, where a copy installed here would never be what resolvers read.

  The swap must then be atomic.

## Authorization

The requester needs the community's super-admin capability, checked against the community's ACL. The spec separates two things:

- **The admin authorises delivery only.** Their capability decides *when* a log is delivered.
- **The log authorises its own content.** Each entry is proven under keys its predecessor committed to, so even full administrative authority can't publish an entry the key holder didn't sign, or move the served log backwards.

## Checks

- `npm run validate` passes for all 470 specs.

| `trust_tasks` | pub.dev | `0.2.1` → `0.2.2` | patch |

What merging does, per registry (all in `publish.yml`, each keyed on "this
version is not published yet"):

- **crates.io** — `release-plz-release` tags `<crate>-v<version>`, publishes in
  dependency order and creates a GitHub Release per crate. Bump levels come from
  `cargo-semver-checks`.
- **npm** — `publish-npm` publishes with OIDC provenance and tags
  `<prefix>-v<version>`.
- **Go** — `publish-go` builds, vets and tests, then pushes the tag, which *is*
  the publication. **Irreversible**: proxy.golang.org never forgets a tag.
- **pub.dev** — `tag-dart` verifies against the *published* core and pushes the
  tag; `publish-dart.yml` publishes from it.

The npm, Go and Dart bumps are only as accurate as the commit subjects — nothing
checks their APIs the way `cargo-semver-checks` checks the crates. Look for a
missing `!` before merging.

This branch is regenerated from `main` on every push, so do not commit to it —
edits are force-pushed away. See RELEASING.md.

title: feat(mediator-transport): the mediator as a Trust-Task counterparty
body:
An Affinidi mediator serves its messaging/* operations as Trust Tasks
addressed to itself. Three kinds of frame come back from it on the session,
and 0.10 handled none of them right:

- its reply is stored as well as pushed, and we never acked a frame from
  the mediator, so every reply stayed in the caller's receive queue and
  replayed on each reconnect. A threaded Trust Tasks envelope from the
  mediator is now acked (isStoredMediatorReply).
- a refusal is a problem report threaded by pthid, which waitFor never
  matched, so it surfaced as a timeout. threadOf keys it by pthid.
- monitor batches are live-only and unthreaded: a new onMediatorMessage
  option keeps them off a consumer's persist-before-ack path, and they are
  no longer buffered for a waiter none can be.

Release 0.11.0.

title: feat(vtc/vetting/vetters/event-mode): the exception to the constant drip (#620)
body:
feat(vtc/vetting/vetters/event-mode): the exception to the constant drip (#620)

A vetter's ordinary rate is a few tokens a tick, whether or not they have
vetted anyone. That is the right rate for ordinary weeks and the wrong one for
a conference desk, and the answer is deliberately not a bigger drip under the
same key: it is a separate token label for a named event, with its own rate,
its own expiry, and a group of vetters large enough that a spend under it still
hides one.

This task carries the vetter's half of that, which is only ever a request. The
approval is an act by someone else, through the community's own administrative
surface, and the specification says why there is no Trust Task for it: a task
the vetter could send is a task a vetter could be made to send.

The response says where the request stands, and carries a group *count* rather
than a group. Who else is at the event is the anonymity set, so the number is
the most a member may be told — enough to tell "nobody has approved it" from
"not enough people have asked", which are the two reasons a request waits.
