title: feat(vtc): add vtc/join-requests/withdraw/0.1 — the applicant closes their own request
body:
Keyring finding KR-03. An applicant could open a join request and then had no
way to close it. A `deferred` request — the community answered `requestMore` —
was the sharp case: it stays open forever, the dedup guard in `submit_inner`
keeps matching the row so no resubmission is possible, and the only exit was
to ask a community admin to reject it, which records the wrong outcome for
what is actually the applicant changing their mind. Nothing but the retention
sweeper ever closed it, on a schedule neither party controls.

The task was spec'd upstream first (dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf #518, shipped in
trust-tasks-rs 0.21.5) and is implemented here against the generated types.
Payload, response and the `withdrawn` status all come from
`trust_tasks_rs::specs::vtc::join_requests::withdraw` — never a local copy.

## Authorization is ownership, not membership

An applicant holds neither a role nor a capability; that is what they are
applying for. So the entitlement is that the proven caller is the applicant
recorded on the request. `resolve_holder` supplies the proof — authcrypt
sender on DIDComm, document proof signer on REST — exactly as `self-remove`
does.

## The two refusals are shaped differently on purpose

  * A request that does not exist and one belonging to somebody else both
    answer `notFound`. Separating them would let a caller probe whether a
    given request id exists on this community — the same enumeration-
    resistance reasoning the vault read paths use.
  * An already-decided request answers `alreadyDecided`, because the applicant
    is entitled to the outcome of their own request and no retry changes it.

Both go out as the extended codes the spec declares rather than through the
generic `AppError` → reject mapping, which flattens `NotFound` and `Gone` into
a bare `taskFailed` carrying only English. Telling "nothing to withdraw" apart
from "already decided" without parsing prose is the whole reason the spec
declares two codes, so a dispatcher-level test pins them.

## requestId is optional

For the same reason it is optional on the status poll: an applicant whose
submit response was lost never received one, and the id-less form is all they
have. A supplied id is preferred over inferring from the caller, as the spec
requires.

## Where the applicant's reason goes

To the audit log, not onto the row. `JoinRequest` is a canonically-typed wire
shape with no member for it, and `decision` means *refusal* — writing it there
would make a withdrawn request read as rejected.
`AuditEvent::JoinRequestWithdrawn` carries the reason alongside the previous
status, and is the one join event whose actor and subject are the same party.
`AuditEvent` is `#[non_exhaustive]`, so the new variant is additive.

## Also, partially, KR-04

The same defect seen from the other side: the duplicate-submit `Conflict` said
"withdraw or await its decision" while naming neither the status nor any
withdraw mechanism. It now names both — `pending` is waiting on the community
and will move on its own, `deferred` is waiting on the applicant and is the
case this task exists for.

KR-04's remaining half is not in this PR and needs an upstream change first:
making that refusal a *typed* answer requires a `requestAlreadyOpen` code on
`vtc/join-requests/submit`, which declares no such code today. Likewise the
second half of KR-03 — letting a deferred applicant supplement the existing
request rather than open a second one — is a task that does not exist yet.
Both are follow-ups.

## Dependency

The `trust-tasks-rs` workspace requirement moves 0.21.4 -> 0.21.5 because
`vta-sdk` re-exports the generated module in its public API, so a consumer
resolving 0.21.4 would not build. The three unrelated lines in Cargo.lock
(`syn`, two `base64`) are pre-existing drift between the committed lock and
what cargo resolves — any `cargo update` of any package rewrites them.

A conformance witness is added in `trust_tasks/conformance.rs`, projected
through the same generated builder the handler returns through rather than
transcribed.

title: fix(tsp): take the SDK's re-establish fix and drop the local copy
body:
Follow-up to #1582, now that the upstream fix has shipped.

## What changes

#1582 worked around a race inside `TspOps::send_reestablishing`: its readiness
read and its `SendInvite` are two separate awaits on the relationship store, and
the peer can move our half between them — its own invite arrives, `None` +
`ReceiveInvite` leaves us `InviteReceived`, and `SendInvite` is legal only from
`None`. The refused invite took the payload down with it, and the D6 recovery
reported a peer that "did not answer" a request it had never been sent.

The workaround was a local copy of the SDK's three steps with the tolerance
added. `affinidi-messaging-sdk` **0.26.12** (affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#838) now
does that re-read itself, so `TspTransport::send_reestablishing` delegates again
and the local `invite_refusal_is_benign` and its three tests are deleted — one
owner for the decision rather than two that can drift.

## Two things the bump settles beyond the deletion

- **`vtc-service` is fixed by it.** Its registry client
  (`registry::messaging::send_tsp`) calls the SDK's form directly and never had
  the workaround. #1582 left it alone because the syncer's backoff — the one
  retry owner on that path — re-sent through the transient failure, so it
  self-healed on the next attempt. Now it does not fail in the first place.
- **The requirement names the patch: `0.26.12`, not `0.26`.** All five
  `affinidi-messaging-sdk` requirements in the workspace move (`vta-sdk`,
  `vta-service`, `vti-common`, `room-host`, `tests/e2e`). On `^0.26` a lockfile
  resolving 0.26.11 would put the race back with nothing local left to catch it
  — the case that makes a floor load-bearing rather than tidy. A patch floor
  costs a downstream nothing.

## What stays from #1582

The part the SDK cannot fix: `recover_send_tsp` telling `Timeout`, `Cancelled`
and `SendFailed(reason)` apart instead of reporting all three as a silent peer,
and the `AnsweringPeer` harness recording what it received and sent. That is
what made the upstream defect readable in one CI run, and it is VTA-side either
way.

## Verification

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| harness tests, 20 consecutive runs under synthetic load (16 spinners) | 20 pass, 0 fail — the delegation carries what the local copy did |
| `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` | 127 targets pass; **one pre-existing failure, see below** |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` | clean, no warnings |
| `cargo fmt --all -- --check` | clean |

## ⚠️ `main` is red before this PR, on something unrelated

`vta-sdk --test generated_wire_types_census` fails on `main` today:

```
1 hand-written type(s) restate a Trust Task that trust-tasks-rs generates:
  ("vtc-service/src/routes/endorsement_types.rs", "EndorsementTypeDeleteResponse"),  // vtc/endorsement-types/delete/0.1
```

`EndorsementTypeDeleteResponse` was added by #1584 — it is not present at that
file's previous commit — and #1584's CI run on `main` was **cancelled**, so
nothing checked it. This branch touches no `vtc-service` file and no census
baseline, so the census result is identical with or without it.

Not fixed here, because it is not a one-liner and it is someone else's endpoint:
the census wants the generated type from `trust_tasks_rs::specs`, and a foreign
type cannot derive `utoipa::ToSchema`, so the REST body needs a wrapper in
`vta_sdk::openapi` (CLAUDE.md, "Trust Task wire types come from
`trust_tasks_rs::specs`"). Worth its own PR.

Design note `tsp-relationship-recovery.md` D6a updated to say where the fix now
lives, and why the floor is a patch version.

title: feat(vtc)!: keep an active admin signed in, and make the idle timeout settable
body:
## The problem

An admin was thrown out of the console on a hard cliff, with no warning and no way to change it — and the cliff was shorter than the config suggested, differing by sign-in door:

- **Passkey sign-in → 300 s.** `routes/auth.rs:738` mints at `acr = "aal2"`, and `access_token_ttl_for_aal2()` returns `max(60, access_ttl/3)`. The cookie's `Max-Age` is that token's remaining life.
- **Wallet/SIOP bridge → up to 900 s.** `/v1/auth/admin-session` mints nothing; it inherits whatever life the presented token had left.

Crucially it was **wall-clock, not idle time**. Working continuously made no difference, because the request path never wrote to the session row (`extractor.rs:144-199` is read-only). The one mechanism that slides a session — `POST /v1/auth/refresh` — takes its token in the request body, sets no cookie, and was unreachable from the SPA: the token is returned only in the passkey-login JSON body, which `Login.tsx:131-139` throws away.

## The design

Tokens stay short and rotating. The idle timeout becomes a **separate server-side policy** measured on `Session.last_seen`:

- `last_seen` advances on **cookie** requests — the operator using the console — and **not** on bearer ones. Bearer callers are the CLIs and service integrations: no idle timeout, and no store write per call.
- `handle_refresh` refuses once `now - last_seen` exceeds the configured timeout.
- The console renews ahead of expiry, seeded from `whoami`'s `session.expiresAt` — a value it already received and ignored.

So token lifetime is a rotation cadence; the idle timeout is the policy. Both sign-in doors behave identically, because the policy lives on the session row rather than the token.

## Three details that are load-bearing

**Refresh no longer resets `last_seen`.** It used to set it to `now`, which would have made the timeout unreachable — the renewal timer would push the deadline out every cycle and the session would never lapse. Rotating a token is the client's timer, not the operator. Safe for the sweeper: `cleanup_expired_sessions` judges refresh-bearing sessions by `refresh_expires_at` and never reads `last_seen`, and the refresh-less intrinsic sessions that *do* use it never reach this handler.

**`/v1/auth/refresh` is no longer CSRF-exempt.** The exemption was sound only while the sole credential was a token in the request body, which an attacker cannot read. A refresh cookie the browser attaches automatically removes that property, and a forged cross-site refresh would rotate the victim's token away — a logout DoS. `has_session_cookie` now recognises both admin cookies, so a body-token refresh (no cookies) still passes unenforced and SDK/CLI clients are untouched. The csrf module's own comment asked for exactly this coupling.

**The `admin-session` refresh token rides in `ext["org.openvtc"]`.** That payload is conformance-checked against `spec/vtc/auth/admin-session/0.1`, which types it as `{accessToken, ext}` — a top-level `refreshToken` would have failed the build. `ext` is the schema's own escape hatch.

## Operator surface

A **Session timeout** card on Access control. It reads `GET /v1/admin/config` and Saves with `PATCH` **then** `POST /v1/admin/config/reload` — PATCH alone persists the db-layer override without touching the running config, so a Save that stopped there would report success and change nothing.

`auth.admin_idle_timeout` is bounded 60 s–86 400 s by a new `ConfigKeyKind::U64Range`, so a scripted `config/patch` is held to the same limits as the console. When the value is pinned by `VTC_AUTH_ADMIN_IDLE_TIMEOUT` the card renders read-only and says so — the env layer outranks the db layer a PATCH writes, so an editable control there would be one whose Save silently did nothing.

Default is **900 s**, deliberately longer than the 300 s cliff it replaces.

## Breaking change

`vti_common::auth::backend::AuthError` gains `SessionIdleTimeout` and is now `#[non_exhaustive]`. The enum has grown with every auth feature and each addition was a silent break for consumers matching exhaustively; marking it costs downstream a wildcard arm once and makes future variants additive.

`SessionStore::touch_session` and `AuthBackend::idle_timeout` are new, **both with default bodies**, so an existing backend compiles unchanged. `touch_session`'s default is a read-modify-write rather than a no-op — a security control must not fail open for a backend that hasn't opted in.

This matters downstream: **did-hosting implements this same `SessionStore` trait** and pins `vti-common 0.18.9`. The version this publishes as is what gates porting the same behaviour there.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vti-common -p vtc-service -p vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — **2192 passed across 68 targets, 0 failed**. Cargo's exit code captured directly (no pipe), full log grepped for `FAILED` / `failures:` / `panicked at`.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean
- `cd vtc-service/admin-ui && npm run test` — 155 passed / 19 files
- `npm run lint` (`wire:check` + `tsc -b --noEmit`) — clean

New: `tests/session_idle_timeout.rs` (12 cases — activity tracking on cookie vs bearer, the window and its config-follows-live behaviour, refresh-is-not-activity, the three-cookie re-issue, CSRF gated vs exempt, sign-out clearing), 4 `config_store` unit tests, 9 `session.ts` tests, 5 `SessionTimeoutCard` tests.

Existing contracts confirmed intact: `cookie_session.rs`, `wallet_login_siop.rs` (incl. "a rejected token emits zero `Set-Cookie`"), `passkey_step_up.rs`, and the `vti-common` session/sweeper suite.

## Not done

- **The aal2 conflation is untouched.** A passkey *login* sets `acr_expires_at = None` — it is not an elevation — yet gets the short elevation TTL. `access_token_ttl_for_aal2` is shared with the VTA, so changing when it applies alters VTA token lifetimes; it deserves its own PR. It no longer decides when an admin is signed out, only how often the token silently rotates.
- **No absolute session cap.** Idle timeout only, by design. There is no anchor to cap against in any case: `created_at` is overwritten on every refresh, so it records the current lease rather than the session's birth.
- **No live browser check.** Verification is the jsdom tests plus the integration suite.

title: feat(vtc)!: keep an active admin signed in, and make the idle timeout settable (#1586)
body:
feat(vtc)!: keep an active admin signed in, and make the idle timeout settable (#1586)

An admin was thrown out of the console on a hard cliff, with no warning and
no way to change it. The cliff was also shorter than the config suggested
and differed by sign-in door: passkey login mints at `acr=aal2`, and the
aal2 access TTL is a third of the base, so the cookie died after 300s —
of wall-clock, not idle time. Working continuously made no difference,
because the request path never wrote to the session row. The first sign of
expiry was a request failing.

Tokens stay short and rotating. The idle timeout becomes a separate
server-side policy measured on `Session.last_seen`:

- `last_seen` advances on cookie-borne requests — the console doing
  something — and not on bearer ones, which are the CLIs and service
  integrations, have no idle timeout, and would otherwise pay a store
  write per call.
- `handle_refresh` refuses once `now - last_seen` exceeds the configured
  timeout, with its own error rather than the generic "authentication
  failed" the other auth failures share. Reaching that point proves
  possession of a valid refresh token, so there is nobody left to withhold
  the reason from, and "you were away" sends an operator somewhere
  different from "your session hit its ceiling".
- The console renews before expiry, single-flight, and re-probes `whoami`
  before declaring a session dead — rotation is atomic, so two tabs
  renewing together means one is refused on a perfectly live session.

Refresh no longer resets `last_seen`. It used to set it to `now`, which
would have made the timeout unreachable: the renewal timer would push the
deadline out on every cycle. Rotating a token is the client's timer, not
the operator. Safe for the sweeper, which judges refresh-bearing sessions
by `refresh_expires_at` and never reads `last_seen`.

`/v1/auth/refresh` is no longer CSRF-exempt. That exemption was sound only
while the sole credential was a token in the request body, which an
attacker cannot read. A refresh cookie the browser attaches automatically
removes the property, and a forged cross-site refresh would rotate the
victim's token away — a logout DoS. Body-token callers carry no session
cookie and still pass unenforced, so SDK and CLI clients are unaffected.

`auth.admin_idle_timeout` joins the runtime config registry, bounded
60s-86400s by a new `U64Range` kind so a scripted `config/patch` is held to
the same limits as the console. Save is PATCH + reload, because PATCH alone
persists the override without touching the running config.

BREAKING CHANGE: `vti_common::auth::backend::AuthError` gains a
`SessionIdleTimeout` variant and is now `#[non_exhaustive]`. The enum has
grown with every auth feature and each addition was a silent break for
consumers matching it exhaustively; marking it costs downstream a wildcard
arm once and makes future variants additive. `SessionStore` gains
`touch_session` and `AuthBackend` gains `idle_timeout`, both with defaults,
so an existing backend compiles unchanged.

title: fix(vtc): return the response wrapper the delete route documents
body:
## `main` is red — this fixes it

`Test (VTC)` fails on `main` at `vtc-service/tests/openapi_response_census.rs`:

```
1 handler(s) document a response body their handler does not return.

  endorsement_types.rs::delete
      declares: EndorsementTypeDelete01Response
      returns:  Json<DeleteTaskResponse>
```

Introduced by #1587. That PR moved the route onto the generated Trust Task type — correctly, to satisfy the `vta-sdk` census — but returned it **bare** while documenting the `spec_types!` wrapper.

The census requires the two to name the same type, and its reasoning is worth restating: the `body =` annotation is what generates the console's `wire.ts`, so a mismatch ships a console reading a shape the daemon never sends — silently, because the generated types typecheck against themselves.

## The fix

`routes::vetting` already shows the shape: return the wrapper, built from the generated value with `.into()`. The wrapper is what carries `ToSchema` for a type this crate does not own, so it is the right thing in the signature as well as in the annotation.

**Only the doc comment moves in `openapi.json`** — the schema `$ref` is unchanged (`VtcEndorsementTypesDeleteV0_1Response` before and after), so the wire contract is identical and no client sees a difference.

## Verification — both jobs this time

| Job | Result |
|---|---|
| `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vtc-client --no-fail-fast` | 63 targets, **1687 tests**, 0 failed, exit 0 |
| `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` | 128 targets, **4652 tests**, 0 failed, exit 0 |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` | clean |
| `cargo fmt --all` | applied |
| `admin-ui`: `npm run lint` | clean, `wire.ts` regenerated and in sync |

Both censuses now pass: `generated_wire_types_census` (3 passed) and `openapi_response_census` (6 passed).

## Why this happened twice

Worth recording, because the two failures are the same mistake in mirror image:

- **#1584** was verified with the VTC job only. `Test (workspace)` is path-filtered and that PR touched only `vtc-service` and `admin-ui`, so the job holding the `vta-sdk` census was never scheduled — and I never ran it locally either.
- **#1587** was verified with the workspace job only. That job **excludes `vtc-service` by definition**, so it could not see `openapi_response_census`.

CLAUDE.md's "Running the tests: green and wrong" lists both commands. Running one of the two, each time the one blind to the problem, is how a correct change landed red twice.

title: spec(vtc/endorsement-types/delete): a criterion requiring the type also blocks its deletion
body:
## What the spec was missing

`vtc/endorsement-types/delete/0.1` described one kind of reference — a live endorsement — and framed `inUse` as being about orphaned endorsements alone.

A second kind exists wherever the consumer also holds admission criteria. A criterion requiring statements of the type is left asking applicants for evidence the community no longer recognises. And where registering such a criterion against an *unregistered* type is itself refused — as it is in the VTC — deleting the type strands the criterion in a state it could not have been created in: still advertised to applicants, and no longer saveable.

## The change

- **`inUse` covers both references**, and gains a `detailsSchema` with `liveEndorsements` (count) and `criteria` (identifiers), so a consumer that can determine both says which applies instead of leaving the caller to parse prose.
- **Both members are optional**, because neither an endorsement store nor a criteria registry is mandatory for a conforming consumer. The spec states plainly that an absent member means *"not applicable here"*, never *"none found"* — a caller must not read silence as an all-clear.
- **Conformance** asks a consumer that can determine both to gather both before refusing. Refusing on the first found turns one determination into as many round trips as there are kinds of reference, each ending in the same code.
- **Security & Privacy** gains what the refusal discloses: `details` names criteria by identifier, a governance fact the authorised administrator can already enumerate, and is reachable only after the community-admin capability has been verified.

## Version

**In place on 0.1**, not a new version folder. The spec is `status: draft`; no payload or response shape changes; no previously-valid document becomes invalid. Per [SPEC §5.2](SPEC.md#52-compatibility-rules) and the version rules in CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.

## Bindings

None regenerate. `payload.schema.json` is untouched, and error codes reach only `website/registry.json`, `website/specs/` and `website/assets/tasks.generated.js` — all gitignored build outputs. Confirmed by grep: no tracked generated file carries `endorsement-types/delete:inUse`.

## Verification

- `npm run validate` — **451 specs validated, 74 shared schemas indexed**, no errors
- `npm run build` — registry and website regenerate cleanly; no tracked file changes beyond `spec.md`
- Error-code casing and shadowing sweeps both report 0 non-conforming

## Implementation

Already implemented in [verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1584](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1584), which added the criterion check and reports both causes in a single refusal. That PR noted the divergence rather than diverging silently; this closes it.

One follow-up remains on the implementation side: it currently carries both causes in the error *message* rather than in structured `details`. Populating `details.liveEndorsements` / `details.criteria` per this schema is a small change there.

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.21.5
body:
### Added

- **vtc/join-requests**: Withdraw/0.1 — an applicant closes their own request ([#518](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/518))

An applicant whose request is answered `requestMore` has no way to end it.
  The community holds it open, the applicant cannot submit another, and the
  only thing that resolves it is a retention sweep neither party controls.

  The registry already assumed this task existed: `join-requests/status/0.1`
  lists `withdrawn` among the states it can report, and nothing could reach
  it. This is the task that does.

  Modelled on `members/self-remove/0.1` — the same shape of act, a subject
  exercising authority over their own record — and scaffolded with
  `npm run new-spec` rather than copied from it, per CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md.

  Three things worth review:

  **`requestId` is OPTIONAL**, following `join-requests/status/0.1` and for
  the same reason: an applicant whose submit response was lost never received
  an id, and would otherwise have no way to reach their own request. A
  consumer given one MUST prefer it over inferring the request from the
  caller.

  **`issuedAt` is REQUIRED for a reason specific to this task**, beyond the
  §7.3 item 17 floor. An applicant may withdraw and then apply again — that
  is the point of it — so a captured withdrawal replayed later does not
  repeat a harmless act: it closes the *next* request, which the applicant
  never withdrew. The two documents are identical apart from when they were
  issued.

  **`notFound` deliberately conflates "no open request" with "not yours"**,
  so a caller cannot probe whether a given request id exists on a community.
  `alreadyDecided` is kept distinct because an applicant is entitled to know
  the outcome of their own request, and because retrying will never change
  it.

  Bindings regenerated for all four targets; `check-bindings` reports 452
  specs against 452 TypeScript, 447 Rust, 452 Go and 452 Dart modules, all
  agreeing. No version or changelog edits — release-plz owns those here.

title: fix(vtc): return the generated endorsement-type delete response, not a copy of it
body:
## `main` is red — this fixes it

`Test (workspace)` fails on `main` at `vta-sdk/tests/generated_wire_types_census.rs`:

```
1 hand-written type(s) restate a Trust Task that trust-tasks-rs generates:
  ("vtc-service/src/routes/endorsement_types.rs", "EndorsementTypeDeleteResponse"),  // vtc/endorsement-types/delete/0.1
```

Introduced by #1584. That PR renamed the route's hand-written response struct out of a three-way `DeleteResponse` collision and, in doing so, gave it a doc comment naming the task it restates — which is exactly what the census matches on. **The type had been violating the census all along**; it was invisible only because it carried no doc comment saying which task it duplicated.

## The fix

The census does not accept new baseline entries, and it is right not to. The handler now returns `trust_tasks_rs::specs::vtc::endorsement_types::delete::v0_1::Response` and constructs it through the generated builder, so a response that does not match the published schema is a construction error rather than a struct literal that compiles and lies.

`utoipa::ToSchema` cannot be derived on a foreign type, so the OpenAPI body is documented with a new `EndorsementTypeDelete01Response` wrapper in `vta_sdk::openapi`, following the same `spec_types!` pattern the vetting family already uses. The published schema becomes `VtcEndorsementTypesDeleteV0_1Response` — rendered from the specification rather than described a second time — and the console's `EndorsementTypeDeleted` alias follows it.

**The JSON body is unchanged**: `{ "typeUri": … }` before and after. No client sees a difference; this is a source-level and OpenAPI change only.

## Why CI missed it on #1584

title: fix(identity): keep the half of a DID that identifies it in the history pane
body:
Follow-up to #360, from a screenshot of the Identity pane's **What has left** tab. The verifier a release went to was named as:

```
did:webvh:QmX38g7H85V9zYdkEucGMcRZbJgyBBWBic
```

No host, no path — and no mark to say it had been cut at all.

## Why this one was worse than the cases #360 fixed

Two separate faults stacked:

1. **The wrong half survived.** A `did:webvh` is told apart from the next one on its host by its path; the SCID is a hash nobody reads and cannot compare by eye. The cut kept the hash.
2. **The cut was invisible.** This pane has its own local `truncate`, which delegates to `truncate_chars` — a bare character cut with no ellipsis. Its doc comment says *"with an ellipsis so a cut is visible"*. It never did that, so a clipped DID was indistinguishable from a whole one. That is what makes the screenshot confusing rather than merely unhelpful: it reads as a complete identifier.

## What changed

`shorten_id` is the identifier truncator for this pane — the `shorten_for_display` added in #360, which gives up the SCID first and only then the middle. Four call sites move onto it:

- **`row.verifier_did`** on the history tab — the reported one.
- **`durable_credential_id`**, the credential id of a release that is still live and still revocable. Two of those differ in their last characters, not their first, and they were being cut at 40 with no ellipsis.
- **`m.community_name`** and **`m.persona_label`** on the Communities tab. Both fall back to a DID when there is no display name or verified agent name, and both were *already* shortened on the way into the view model (`shorten_did`, now DID-aware) and then blunt-cut again here at 30 and 24 — which threw the path away a second time. Two-stage shortening is fine as long as both stages know what a DID is; now they do.

The local `truncate` stays for prose (display names, claim types, values — text that reads from the front), but it now goes through `truncate_did`, so it finally does what its doc comment has always claimed and marks the cut.

## Verification

`cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace`, and `cargo test --workspace -- --include-ignored` are all green.

One new test, pinned to the shape in the report: a verifier DID with a real SCID, host and path renders with `dids.ic3.dev:decade-equip` intact, without `QmX38g7H85V9zYdkEucGMcRZbJgyBBWBic`, and with a visible `…`; the still-live credential id keeps its trailing `5a7cac05b0d6`.

Not verified live — a rendering change validated by the panel's render tests, not by a run against the services.

## Pre-merge checklist

```
- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2) — n/a, rendering only
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3) — n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1) — n/a, no mutations
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4) — n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5) — n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6) — n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*) — none
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*) — n/a
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*) — the point of the change: a truncated identifier no longer presents itself as a whole one
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1) — n/a
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers — none
```

title: feat(vtc/join-requests): withdraw/0.1 — an applicant closes their own request
body:
## The gap

An applicant whose join request is answered `requestMore` cannot end it. The community holds it open, the applicant cannot submit another (communities cap open requests per applicant), and the only thing that resolves it is a retention sweep neither party controls.

**The registry already assumed this task existed.** `join-requests/status/0.1` lists `withdrawn` among the states it can report — and nothing in the registry could reach it. This is the task that does.

Reported against an implementation as **VTI-03** by the Keyring wallet team at the Berkman Center, who hit it with a deferred request during onboarding.

## Shape

Modelled on `members/self-remove/0.1` — the same kind of act, a subject exercising authority over their own record — and scaffolded with `npm run new-spec` rather than copied from it, per CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md.

Classifications: `sideEffects: mutating` (ends an open request and releases the applicant to apply again; nothing is erased, so not `destructive`), `exposure: { discloses: none, actsAsSubject: true }`, `retention: durable`. Consequential, so proof and `issuedAt` are REQUIRED.

## Three decisions worth review

**`requestId` is OPTIONAL**, following `join-requests/status/0.1` and for the same reason: an applicant whose submit response was lost never received an id, and would otherwise have no way to reach their own request. A consumer that is given one MUST prefer it over inferring the request from the caller.

**`issuedAt` is REQUIRED for a reason specific to this task**, beyond the §7.3 item 17 floor that already applies. An applicant may withdraw and then apply again — that is the point of the task — so a captured withdrawal replayed later does not repeat a harmless act: **it closes the next request, which the applicant never withdrew.** The two documents are identical apart from when they were issued, so `issuedAt` is the only thing that distinguishes them.

**`notFound` deliberately conflates "you have no open request" with "that id is not yours."** Distinguishing them would let a caller probe whether a given request id exists on a community. `alreadyDecided` is kept distinct, because an applicant is entitled to know the outcome of their own request and because retrying will never change it.

## Authorization

The entitlement is ownership — the applicant may withdraw *their own* request and no other — and the `## Authorization` section says so explicitly rather than describing the verification pipeline. It is deliberately not membership, a capability or an invitation: an applicant holds none of those, which is why they are applying.

## Verification

- `npm run validate` — 452 specs, 74 shared schemas, 681 example documents; no errors
- `npm run check-bindings` — 452 specs against 452 TypeScript, 447 Rust, 452 Go and 452 Dart modules, all agreeing
- `cargo test --workspace` — 872 passed, 0 failed
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features "validate,vtc" vtc::join_requests::withdraw` — **3 tests**, which is the count that means the fixtures actually ran (`--features validate` alone compiles no `vtc/*` and reports a green zero)
- The four `payload.invalid-examples.json` fixtures were **verified to bite**: making one of them valid and regenerating turns `rejects_invalid_examples` red. Fixtures are baked at codegen time, so editing the JSON without re-running the generator tests nothing — worth knowing, as it makes a negative check silently vacuous.
- `npm run build`

No version or changelog edits — release-plz owns those here.

## Follow-on

The implementing side (`vtc-service` in OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure) already has `JoinStatus::Withdrawn` declared, handled by its retention sweeper, and unreachable — the duplicate-application guard releases on it. That work waits on this spec and a `trust-tasks-rs` release.

title: fix(vtc): move "Request member VMC" to the Credentials card it acts on
body:
## What

Moves the **Request member VMC** button from the Admin actions card up to the bottom of **Credentials**, directly under the Membership edge row.

## Why

The button changes one thing — whether the membership edge is complete — and it sat four cards below that row, past Published relationships, Disposition + consent and Vetter role, in a block otherwise about promoting and removing people. Asking a member for their half of the pair is neither.

The Membership edge copy already read *"…Request a fresh one below"*, which was a cross-card reference to a button an operator had to go hunting for. It now points at something adjacent.

The mutation's error and success feedback came along. Left behind, a click in Credentials would have reported its result four cards down and out of view. No behaviour change: same mutation, same handler, same disabled state and title text.

## Verification

- `cd vtc-service/admin-ui && npm run test` — 141 passed / 17 files
- `npm run lint` (`wire:check` + `tsc -b --noEmit`) — clean

title: feat(vtc): remove a statement type from Vetting → Requirements, and say what depends on it
body:
## What

The Requirements page could register a statement type but never remove one. Now it can, and each type says which criteria depend on it.

- **Unused** → `No criterion requires it.`, Remove enabled.
- **In use** → `Required by criteria kernel-developer, contributor. Remove or re-point them first.`, Remove disabled. The note is the button's `aria-describedby`, so the reason is not tooltip-only.
- **Criteria not yet loaded** → `Checking which criteria require it…`, Remove disabled rather than guessing "nothing uses this".

Removal goes through a confirm dialog; the daemon's 409 renders verbatim in the error block, which is where the live-statement count surfaces (counting it client-side would mean paging the whole endorsement store).

## Why the criteria, and not live endorsements

The card previously explained that removal was withheld because the console could not see what referenced a type. The half it *can* see is the half that blocks an operator in practice: peer-vetting statements are signed by vetters' own wallets and never enter this community's endorsement store, so the live count is usually zero. What actually depends on a statement type is an Accepts criterion naming it — and the Requirements page has already loaded every criterion.

## The correctness gap this closes

`POST /v1/schemas/accepts` refuses a criterion whose `statementType` is not registered (`routes/schemas.rs:238-250`), but the delete handler only counted live endorsements. A delete could therefore strand a criterion in exactly the state registration forbids: still advertising a type the community no longer recognises, and no longer saveable.

`DELETE /v1/endorsement-types/{uri}` now gathers **both** references and reports them in one 409, rather than making the operator clear one and discover the other:

```
endorsement-type-in-use: '<uri>' is still referenced — 2 live endorsement(s)
of it exist; criteria 'kernel-developer', 'contributor' require statements of
it. Revoke the endorsements and remove or re-point the criteria before
deleting the type.
```

Adding the guard server-side rather than UI-only means a scripted `DELETE` cannot strand a criterion either.

## A documentation defect fixed on the way

Three structs in `vtc-service` are named `DeleteResponse` (`routes/schemas.rs`, `routes/website/files.rs`, `routes/endorsement_types.rs`). utoipa's component registry keeps one, and `routes::schemas`' `{ id }` won — so `openapi.json` documented this route as returning `{ id }` when it returns `{ typeUri }`, and the console's generated `wire.ts` carried that error. Renamed to `EndorsementTypeDeleteResponse`, and the path got a real `operation_id` (it was the bare `"delete"`). **The JSON body is unchanged** — this is an OpenAPI fix only.

## Specification note

`spec/vtc/endorsement-types/delete/0.1` describes the 409 as the live-endorsement case only. The new condition adds no wire shape and reuses the same `endorsement-type-in-use` code, but it is behaviour the specification does not yet state and should reach dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf. Flagging rather than diverging silently.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — **1687 passed across 63 targets, 0 failed** (cargo exit code captured directly, full log grepped for `FAILED` / `failures:` / `panicked at`)
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean
- `cd vtc-service/admin-ui && npm run test` — 145 passed / 17 files
- `npm run lint` (`wire:check` + `tsc -b --noEmit`) — clean

New coverage: `delete_type_refused_while_a_criterion_names_it` (asserts the 409 names the criterion, and that removing it releases the type — the guard is not sticky), three unit tests on the refusal message, and four admin-UI cases covering the enabled/disabled/unknown states and the 409 render.

Two `RequirementsPanel` tests were matching criterion ids by bare text and became ambiguous once the card renders those ids too; re-anchored on the criterion card's own heading.

## Not done

No live browser check — verification is the jsdom component tests asserting the rendered DOM including the disabled states.

title: fix(tsp): a peer's invite landing mid-recovery must not lose the resend
body:
`d6_recovers_a_reply_from_an_answering_peer` has failed **six of the last ten
`Test (workspace)` runs on `main`** (and on the release PR #1570, which inherits
it). It is not a flaky test: it is a real defect that fires about half the time.

## The defect

The D6 reply-timeout recovery (`recover_send_tsp`) resets our half of the TSP
relationship and re-establishes it with the payload riding behind the invite
(§3.6). `TspOps::send_reestablishing` does that in three steps, and the first
two are separate awaits on the relationship store: read the send readiness, then
`SendInvite`. The peer can move our half in between — its own invite arrives,
`None` + `ReceiveInvite` leaves us `InviteReceived`, and `SendInvite` is legal
only from `None`. The invite is then refused with

```
invalid transition: SendInvite in state InviteReceived
```

and the payload is never sent.

That is not a failed recovery. It is the outcome the invite existed to produce,
reached from the other side: a relationship is on record again, and
`admits_application_message()` is true for every state but `None`. And the
collision is commonest exactly where recovery is — two endpoints repairing the
same broken relationship at once is what a mediator restart or a VTA redeploy
produces.

## The fix

`TspTransport::send_reestablishing` spells the three steps out rather than
calling the SDK's combined form, and answers a refused invite by re-reading the
store rather than by matching on the error's text: our half no longer `None`
means carry on to the payload; still `None` means the invite failed for its own
reasons and that error stands. The payload is sent exactly once either way.

`invite_refusal_is_benign` carries that decision as a pure function with its own
tests. The race itself lives between two awaits inside the SDK and cannot be
staged in a test — forcing the store to `InviteReceived` beforehand does not
reproduce it, because the readiness read then answers `HandshakeInFlight` and no
invite is attempted at all — so the decision is what gets pinned. Same split as
`tsp_inbound::decide_control`.

## Two diagnosis defects, both fixed here

The failure was unreadable, which is why it survived six merges:

- `recover_send_tsp` collapsed `Timeout`, `Cancelled` and `SendFailed(reason)`
  into "`<peer>` did not answer over TSP after re-establishing the
  relationship". A frame that never left this VTA was reported as a silent peer,
  sending every reader to the wrong endpoint. The steady-state `send_tsp` beside
  it already told the three apart.
- The `AnsweringPeer` harness discarded every fault inside its loop — `Err(_) =>
  break` on the socket, `let _ = send_document(…)` on the reply. It now records
  what it received and sent, and the assertion prints it; `received 0
  document(s)` is what named the cause.

Also corrected a doc comment on `AnsweringPeer` that became stale hours after it
was written: the ACL grant no longer decides that test, because the spine now
classifies an inbound document and hands a threaded one to its waiter before any
ACL check.

## Verification

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| harness tests, 20 consecutive runs under synthetic load (16 spinners, load avg 30–48) | 20 pass, 0 fail |
| same loop before the fix | failed on the first loaded run, with the message above |
| `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` | green |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` | clean, no warnings |
| `cargo fmt --all -- --check` | clean |

The CI timestamps are what ruled out the obvious reading. The test's reply
budget is 5 s and it failed ~1 s after starting, so nothing ever waited for a
reply — the send had failed outright.

## Not fixed here, deliberately

The same race is open in `vtc-service`'s registry client
(`registry::messaging::send_tsp`), which still calls the SDK's combined form.
There it surfaces as a transient `Unreachable` and the syncer's backoff — the
one retry owner on that path — re-sends into a store that by then reads
`HandshakeInFlight`, so it self-heals on the next attempt. A one-shot recovery
has no such owner, which is why the VTA's arm could not. Recorded in the design
note.

The cleaner long-term fix is upstream: make the SDK's readiness-read-and-invite
atomic per `(our_vid, their_vid)`.

Design note: `docs/05-design-notes/tsp-relationship-recovery.md` D6a.

That is not a failed recovery. It is the outcome the invite existed to produce,
reached from the other side: a relationship is on record again, and
`admits_application_message()` is true for every state but `None`. And the
collision is commonest exactly where recovery is — two endpoints repairing the
same broken relationship at once is what a mediator restart or a VTA redeploy
produces.

So `TspTransport::send_reestablishing` spells the three steps out rather than
calling the SDK's combined form, and answers a refused invite by re-reading the
store rather than by matching on the error's text: our half no longer `None`
means carry on to the payload; still `None` means the invite failed for its own
reasons and that error stands. The payload is sent exactly once either way.
`invite_refusal_is_benign` carries that decision as a pure function with its own
tests — the race itself lives between two awaits inside the SDK and cannot be
staged in a test, so the decision is what gets pinned.

Found through `d6_recovers_a_reply_from_an_answering_peer`, which had failed six
of the last ten `Test (workspace)` runs on main. The answering peer's
spawn-time `relate` is the colliding invite and the window is two store reads,
so it is a coin flip under load — and it never showed in the isolated
`transport-harness` step, only in the full parallel suite.

Two diagnosis defects made it unreadable, both fixed here:

- `recover_send_tsp` collapsed `Timeout`, `Cancelled` and `SendFailed(reason)`
  into "`<peer>` did not answer over TSP after re-establishing the
  relationship", so a frame that never left this VTA was reported as a silent
  peer and sent every reader to the wrong endpoint. The steady-state `send_tsp`
  beside it already told the three apart.
- The `AnsweringPeer` harness discarded every fault inside its loop — `Err(_) =>
  break` on the socket, `let _ = send_document(…)` on the reply. It now records
  what it received and sent, and the assertion prints it; `received 0
  document(s)` is what named the cause.

The same race is open in `vtc-service`'s registry client, which calls the SDK's
combined form. There it surfaces as a transient `Unreachable` and the syncer's
backoff — the one retry owner on that path — re-sends into a store that by then
reads `HandshakeInFlight`, so it self-heals on the next attempt. Left as is
deliberately; a one-shot recovery has no such owner, which is why the VTA's arm
could not.

Design note: `docs/05-design-notes/tsp-relationship-recovery.md` D6a.

title: fix(resolver): take the shared DID resolver instead of building one
body:
Closes KR-19 (their **VTI-19**) — one command fetching `/.well-known/did.jsonl` forty times in five minutes, earning a 429 from the DID host's own rate limiter.

## Two problems, not one

**Twelve call sites each constructed their own `DIDCacheClient`.** A client owns its cache, so the same DID was fetched once per *construction* rather than once per process. `vta-service/src/webvh_cli.rs` alone had five.

**And by calling `DIDCacheClient::new` directly, none of them read `PNM_RESOLVER_URL`.** So an operator who had configured a resolver sidecar — the documented mitigation for exactly this load — did not get it on any of these paths. That env var exists precisely so a single setting reaches every resolver construction without breaking the SDK's public API (see the module doc on `vta-sdk/src/resolver.rs`), and these sites went around it.

The second is the more consequential of the two: the first multiplies fetches, the second removes the thing an operator would reach for to absorb them.

## Why the conversion is behaviour-preserving

Every converted site built

```rust
DIDCacheConfigBuilder::default()
    .with_host_policy(vta_sdk::resolver::webvh_host_policy())
    .build()
```

which is byte-for-byte what `build_did_cache_config(None)` produces. So `shared_did_resolver_from_env()` is a drop-in that additionally honours the env var, and the twelve caches collapse into the one the SDK already keeps per (runtime, sidecar URL, host policy).

## Three sites deliberately left alone

Each looks convertible, and none is:

- **`vtc-service/src/server.rs`** and **`room-host/src/main.rs`** build a plain default with **no host policy**. Converting them would add `webvh_host_policy()` and change which hosts are permitted — a security-relevant change, not a caching one.
- **`pnm-cli/src/bootstrap.rs`** passes `None` **on purpose**. `bootstrap connect` resolves the DID locally so the operator verifies the SCID and signed log on their own machine rather than trusting a sidecar; CLAUDE.md records this explicitly. That `None` is the trust boundary, not an oversight. It is the single most convertible-looking construction in the tree.

This is why each site's config was read rather than the constructor pattern-matched.

## The test that was missing

All of the above now rests on `shared_did_resolver` actually sharing, and nothing pinned that. If sharing broke, every converted site would quietly revert to a private cache with no test failing — the same shape as the bug being fixed.

`two_callers_on_one_runtime_share_one_resolver` asserts on the registry rather than on cache hits: counting fetches against a loopback DID would need the private-host policy and make the test as much about host policy as about sharing.

It is feature-gated (`resolver` sits behind `session`/`didcomm`/`tsp`/…), so I checked it runs in CI's workspace job rather than assuming: it does, via feature unification — 876 tests compile under `--workspace` versus 380 for `-p vta-sdk` alone, which is the discrepancy CLAUDE.md warns about.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — 399 passed, 0 failed
- `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — 1110 passed, 0 failed
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean

No version edits: release-plz owns those here, and a red semver report on this PR would be the report working.

and host policy.

  default with no host policy. Converting them would add

  the DID locally so the operator verifies the SCID and signed log on
  their own machine rather than trusting a sidecar; that `None` is the

that two callers on one runtime get one resolver. Sharing could have
broken and every converted site would have quietly gone back to a private
cache with nothing failing.

Reported as VTI-19 by the Keyring wallet team, who saw one command fetch
`/.well-known/did.jsonl` forty times in five minutes.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* test(resolver): count shared resolvers for this runtime, not the process

The sharing test asserted `after == before + 1` over the whole registry
and failed in CI. The registry is process-global and every other
`#[tokio::test]` in the binary registers under its own runtime key, so a
total is noisy — and, the part that actually broke it, not monotonic:
`shared_did_resolver` prunes entries whose runtime has ended *before* it
inserts, so a call that adds one entry can also remove several. CI hit
exactly that, pruning a dead entry in the same call that added ours and
leaving the count unchanged.

Count only the entries keyed to the current runtime. That is immune to
what any other test has registered or left behind, and it is the property
the test is about: this runtime asks twice and gets one resolver.

The 0 -> 1 -> still-1 sequence is also what stops it passing vacuously —
if registration were broken the count would stay 0, and if sharing were
broken it would reach 2. An earlier draft proved that by registering a
second key with a different sidecar URL, which put the client in network
mode and made the test spend five seconds waiting on a socket that is not
the subject. It runs in 0.02s without it.

title: test(transport-harness): give the d6 success arm room for a real round trip
body:
`d6_recovers_a_reply_from_an_answering_peer` is flaking in **`Test (workspace)`** — the job this repo's own CI comments call *"the gate that matters"*.

## It is not a new break

| Run | Commit | Result |
|---|---|---|
| [35465791169](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/actions/runs/35465791169) — **main**, 19 Sep 19:54 | `73509892` | **failed on this test** |
| 35466562292 — **main**, 19 Sep 20:10 | `89ebd895` | green |

Same test, opposite outcomes on `main`, sixteen minutes apart. It has also failed twice on #1581, which touches nothing near it — including once on a re-run of identical code, while `Feature combos` went green on that same re-run.

## Why it flakes

The test bounded its reply wait at 5s, with a comment explaining the bound is "generous relative to the orphan tests" because it must cover a real round trip: re-invite → deliver → the peer's reply → the VTA correlating it.

**That bound is a fixture parameter, not the subject.** What the test asserts is the *correlation* — that the answering peer's reply is matched through `pending_replies` and returned, so the coordinator records a success rather than a give-up. The timeout only has to be long enough not to fire first.

At 5s it was also asserting, in effect, that a loaded CI runner completes a TSP round trip within five seconds. It does not reliably do that.

## Why 30s weakens nothing

A reply that never arrives still fails the assertion — it just takes longer to say so. And the timeout path keeps its own dedicated coverage in `d6_drives_recovery_on_a_reply_timeout`, which uses a silent orphan peer and a deliberately short bound, so nothing about timeout behaviour is being relaxed here.

The healthy path is unaffected: the harness still completes in ~7.5s locally, because the wait ends when the reply arrives, not when the bound elapses.

## Why fix it rather than re-run past it

The cost of a flaky test in this job is not the re-run. It is that it teaches people a red `Test (workspace)` means nothing — and this repo already has the incident that follows from that, with six consecutive PRs merging onto a red `main` in September. CLAUDE.md's "a merge is not evidence that anything passed" section exists because of it.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vta-service --features transport-harness transport_harness_tests` — **9/9 pass**
- `cargo clippy -p vta-service --features transport-harness --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean

Test-only; no version edits (release-plz owns those here).

Found while investigating #1581's red, which this unblocks.

title: fix(step-up): route delegated pushes to an approver's own mediator
body:
## What

`approver_mediator` returned `None` for any DID that was not `did:key`, so a `did:webvh` or `did:peer` approver was never pushed to. All four call sites give up at that point — `consent_request.rs:195` and `:329`, `consent.rs:385`, `step_up.rs:856` — and each sits **upstream of everything that would otherwise reach the device**: the TSP attempt, the DIDComm forward, and `trigger_gateway_wake`.

One gate therefore starved three delivery paths at once, which is why the symptom presented from several directions: a consent request that stayed queued, an idle approver that was never roused, and a delegated step-up that fell back to the relay every time.

The predicate now resolves the approver's DID document and reads the mediator from its `DIDCommMessaging` service, matching on service `type` per the workspace transport rules. `did:key` keeps its existing behaviour — it cannot advertise a service, so it routes through the VTA's configured mediator, where the holder registered it.

## Two decisions worth review

**A routable approver never falls back to the configured mediator.** Forwarding to a mediator the approver is not registered with does not reach them, and spends a slot of this VTA's sender-queue allowance to do nothing — the shared-fate shape behind the mediator queue-cap failure. `None` (relay fallback) is the honest answer.

**Resolution is bounded by a 5s timeout.** Every call site awaits this inline on a request path (`step_up.rs:1226`, `:1277`) while the push it gates is documented as best-effort and never a hard dependency, so an approver whose DID host is slow must not hold the caller's response open. The shared `AppState::did_resolver` is used rather than a fresh resolver, so its cache absorbs repeat pushes to the same approver.

## Also

- The three call sites that read `[messaging] mediator_did` under the config read-lock now clone it and drop the lock first: the route decision is network I/O, and holding the lock across it would stall config writers.
- Corrected a warning in `consent_request.rs` that told operators "a non-`did:key` approver produces this" — true before this change, false after.

## Testing

- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — 1770 passed, 0 failed
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- Both reduced-feature clippy runs CI performs (`--features rest`, which has neither `didcomm` nor `tsp`, and `setup,keyring,rest,tsp,cli-synthesis`) — clean
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean
- New unit tests cover the routable-DID route, and that a routable approver does not fall back to our mediator. The existing test pinning the old `did:key`-only behaviour was rewritten against the pure decision function.

## Not covered here

Live validation against a `did:webvh` mediator with a phone-shaped approver — that is the acceptance test for this fix and has not been run yet.

Reported as VTI-26 and VTI-24 by the Keyring wallet team, who hit it with `did:webvh` phone approvers.

title: fix(vta)!: answer the contexts family's declared error codes, and stop distinguishing "not yours" from "not there"
body:
Started as "implement `vta/contexts/delete:notEmpty`". Reading the family's specifications turned it into something larger, because the codes are not the interesting part.

## The leak

Every id-taking task in `vta/contexts/*` checked scope and existence separately, and reported them separately:

```rust
auth.require_context(id)?;                       // 403 — and names the id back
get_context(..).ok_or(AppError::NotFound(..))?;  // 404
```

So a caller scoped to one context learned, from which refusal came back, exactly which other context ids exist. Here is the real thing, captured from the disproving run:

```json
"code": "permissionDenied",
"message": "permission denied: forbidden: no access to context: cov-real"
```

`create_context` had it inverted — parent looked up *before* the scope check — so an unauthorised caller learned a parent was real before being told it couldn't use it.

The specifications require the opposite and say so outright. `vta/contexts/get`: *"deliberately does not distinguish 'does not exist' from 'exists but not yours'"*. `update`, `update-did` and `delete` each repeat it as *"whether or not it exists"*. `create` names `parentNotFound` and ties it to `get`'s reasoning.

## What changed

**`reach_context`** — the family's single answer to "does this caller get to act on this id". Scope, then existence, one `Unreachable` for both. Six operations go through it; `create` gets the same for its parent.

**One `reject_context_error`** maps the typed error to the code the *calling* task declares. The slug is read off the document, so these are all the same match:

| task | code |
|---|---|
| `get` | `vta/contexts/get:notFound` |
| `update` | `vta/contexts/update:notFound` |
| `update-did` | `vta/contexts/update-did:notFound` |
| `preview-delete` | `vta/contexts/preview-delete:notFound` |
| `delete` | `vta/contexts/delete:notFound`, `:notEmpty` |
| `create` | `vta/contexts/create:parentNotFound` |

`From`/`Into` keeps `?` working inside the operations and converts back for the transports that carry a status rather than a Trust-Task code, so REST and DIDComm needed no per-site changes.

**`delete:notEmpty`** lands here too. It rode out as `malformedRequest` — which says the request was wrong, when it was well-formed, understood, and refused for what the context holds. The refusal now counts the whole subtree instead of saying `"associated resources"` (as true of one key as of forty) and carries the counts in `details`.

## Deliberately not changed

**`vta/contexts/secrets` keeps entitlement-before-existence.** Its specification argues that ordering rather than inheriting `get`'s: *"not found is only ever said to a caller already entitled to hear it, so the pair leaks nothing"*. `entitlement_is_checked_before_existence` already pins it. Conflating it would have broken a deliberate design. Its two codes stay unimplemented — `export.rs` has three distinct sources of `NotFound` and that wants reading, not pattern-matching.

**The cheap approach was wrong and I took the typed one.** Mapping every `AppError::NotFound` in these handlers to `<task>:notFound` would have been a few lines — but `delete_context` drives `delete_did_webvh_with`, whose `NotFound` means a DID record is missing. That would answer "no such context" for a DID that vanished mid-cascade.

## Tests

Each confirmed to fail without the fix.

- **`every_contexts_task_answers_its_own_not_found`** — per task, asserts the code *and* that a real-but-unreachable id and an absent one come back identical. Asserted on the emitted document; the refusal being typed internally is not evidence anything puts the code on the wire.
- **`a_delete_without_force_answers_not_empty_on_the_wire`** — same reasoning for `notEmpty` (failed with `taskFailed`).
- The `create` and `delete` pairs at the operations layer assert `to_string()` equality, not just the same variant: a message naming one of them hands back what the variant hides.
- Controls, so neither "always refuses" nor "everything is notFound now" could pass: `an_empty_leaf_needs_no_force`, `top_level_creation_requires_super_admin` (a role question, still `Forbidden`).

## Breaking

A caller scoped elsewhere now gets `notFound` / **404** where it got `permissionDenied` / **403** — on get, update-did, preview-delete, delete, and create's parent. That is the change, not a side effect of it.

`context_admin_cannot_update_other_context_did` asserted the 403. It was right about the authorisation and wrong about what to tell the caller; it now asserts 404 for a real id *and* an absent one, and that the refusal modified nothing.

## Verification

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- webvh-off build (`--no-default-features --features rest,didcomm`) — clean
- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — **128 targets, 0 failures** (re-run after the integration-test update; the prior run was 127 green plus the one expected 403→404 failure).

Expect `semver report` red: `create_context`, `get_context_op`, `update_context`, `update_context_did`, `preview_delete_context` and `delete_context` change their error type.

`delete_did_webvh_with`, whose `NotFound` means a DID record is missing, and
that would answer "no such context" for a DID that vanished mid-cascade.
Hence the typed error.

## Breaking

A caller scoped elsewhere now receives `notFound` / HTTP 404 where it
received `permissionDenied` / 403, on get, update-did, preview-delete,
delete and create-parent. That is the point of the change, and it is a
change in what existing callers see.

`context_admin_cannot_update_other_context_did` asserted the 403. It was
right about the authorisation and wrong about what to tell the caller; it
now asserts 404 for both a real id and an absent one.

title: fix(ux): take the questions off the screens that were guessing at them
body:
Seven findings from a live UX run, and the answer to most of them is that a screen was asking for something it could work out, or naming a key it had not bound.

## Creating a persona

**The label.** "Label for the new persona:" over an empty box said what to fill in and nothing about what it is for. It now says, in one line, that it is a name for you, that it names the context its keys live in, and that communities are shown the DID instead — and the empty field carries an example (`e.g. Work, Conference, Alice`) as a dimmed placeholder that is gone the moment anything is typed.

> The report suggested `openvtc-alice` as the placeholder, read off the "a context of its own" line on the screen behind. That string is the account's **top context id**, not anything derived from the label, so using it would have taught the wrong thing.

**The path.** The screen put a permanent, public, possibly-taken name next to a random one and left the reader to work out which mattered. The server-assigned outcome is now the whole screen, with the note that a memorable name does not have to live in the DID — an **agent name** points at it and can be changed later. The typed path is still reachable behind `p`; inside that editor Esc means "let the server pick", not "back to the label".

**The context.** Which VTA context a persona is minted into is no longer asked at all. Every persona gets a sub-context of its own, named from its label: it is the only answer that keeps the isolation the sub-context exists for, and it was being put to someone who had just been told what a `did:webvh` path is.

That removal reaches three screens for the price of one. `community_context::context_options` already collapses to a single option for any persona whose keys live somewhere, so the Context row on the join's vetting page and the context field on the new-application form had one reachable value for everything but a brand-new persona. Both are gone; `context_index` stays at 0, which is the value those rows opened on.

## Identifiers on screen

A `did:webvh` is told apart from the next one on its host by its **path**, and every truncation in the tree dropped exactly that:

```
did:webvh:QmZBWtbz1VVTwyFNUHjx8YfL9fZ8XDc6KrBQ66tj9xq6Eh:dids.ic3.dev:firstperson-vtc
did:webvh:QmZBWtbz1VVTwyFNUHjx8YfL9fZ8XDc6KrB...          ← before, at 48
did:webvh:QmZB…q6Eh:dids.ic3.dev:firstperson-vtc          ← after, at 48
```

New `openvtc_core::display::shorten_for_display` gives up the SCID first (via the existing `shorten_webvh`, which parses with `didwebvh-rs` per the repo rule) and only then the middle, spending the remaining budget on the tail. `display_identifier`, `community_label`, `shorten_did`, `membership_profile_label`, `log_did` and the setup/loading screens all go through it.

## Joining

`asdasd` reached the vetting page, failed to resolve, and was offered **"join anyway — the way forward here"**: an offer to address a request to nothing.

- `validate_join_input` returns `Result` now and refuses anything that is neither a DID nor an agent name, naming what was typed. The DID check is deliberately shallow — a method-specific id is the method's business, and refusing a method this build has not heard of would refuse a community OpenVTC can reach.
- A *well-formed* DID that resolves to nothing is a different failure from a community that will not answer, and `learn_over_http` now returns a `NotLearned` enum saying which. An unresolvable DID gets its own page, without the `j` key, saying to check the DID with whoever gave it to you. A **timeout** stays on the resolvable side: slow is not absent (R6.4).

## Vetting

**The frozen screen.** The holder-grant view ends "then press `f` again" — and `f` was not bound there. It is a List-tab verb, and that view is a form mode, where only Esc/Enter/Tab/arrows and a few mode-guarded letters exist. With no field to type in and no rows to move between, Tab and the arrows did nothing visible either, so the whole view read as frozen and only a restart got back to a working `f`. `f` now retries, and the footer names both keys.

**A refusal nobody could see.** `Intake::Refused` sent a reply and no `Notice`, so a vetter whose applicant was turned away saw an empty desk — the one person who can issue a fresh ticket learned nothing. There is now a `Notice::RequestRefused` reaching their activity log (informational, no inbox task), and a shared `queries::request_refusal_words` turns the code into a sentence on **both** ends, in place of `vetting/request:invalidTicket` printed under a vetter's name (R6.4). The `Silent` branch stays silent: it exists so a guesser cannot discover the vetter, and a log line they could provoke would hand them the same discovery from the other side.

> I could not determine the root cause of the reported refusal from the screenshots, and one thing in them is the clue: **the vetter's Tickets count was 0** while the applicant held a link naming him. The only code path that removes a ticket was `d` on the Tickets view — one keypress, next to `u` and `y`, which copy — and everyone already holding that ticket is refused from then on and cannot be told. It is confirmed now, and the confirmation says that is the cost. If it recurs, check first whether the two panes are the same profile.

**Asking a vetter is one field.** The ticket link carries the vetter's DID, so the separate box for it only ever held what the paste was about to overwrite. Ctrl+V works on that field now (it previously typed a literal `v`), and the vetter read out of the link is *shown* rather than typed — seeing where the request is about to go is the check a person can actually make on a string of base64.

> Consequence, chosen deliberately: a spoken short code alone can no longer reach a vetter, since nothing else would carry their DID. `normalise_code` is now unreachable from the applicant UI, and the vetter's own "read it to the person" wording was replaced with "press ⏎ to show its QR code, or u to copy its link" so the two ends do not contradict each other. Core still accepts a `ShortCodeTicket` on the wire, so interop is unchanged.

## Verification

`cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace`, and `cargo test --workspace -- --include-ignored` are all green. New tests cover each finding: the label and path screens' rendering and keys, the persona sub-context, `shorten_for_display` keeping two DIDs on one host apart, `validate_join_input`'s table, the unresolvable-DID page withholding `j`, `f` on the holder-grant view, the one-field request form, and the vetter hearing about a refused request.

Not verified live — this is a TUI change set validated by rendering and key-routing tests, not by a run against the services.

## Pre-merge checklist

```
- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2) — no new clients; the resolve keeps its RESOLVE_TIMEOUT
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3) — n/a, no new locks
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1) — the persona mint is unchanged; the ticket delete is local-only and now confirmed
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4) — n/a, no new retries
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5) — n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6) — n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*) — no wire types changed; Notice is internal
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*) — an unresolvable community DID now fails closed (no join offered) rather than open
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*) — a refused vetting request now reaches the vetter's log; both ends say what the code means rather than printing it
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1) — the ticket delete persists through the same coalesced save as before, behind a confirmation
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers — none
```

title: ci: filter Feature combos by what it builds, and give it a budget it fits in
body:
Two changes to the longest job on the graph. Asked for as "gate it" and "raise the timeout"; the first turned out to need a split before it was safe.

## The filter could not simply be added

`affects` already gates `Mobile build`, `Enclave build` and both test jobs. `Feature combos` — the most expensive of the lot — had no filter at all, so every docs-only and CLI-only PR waited ~45 minutes for it.

Adding the obvious gate would have been **wrong**. Twenty of its steps name their package with `-p`; one did not:

```
cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings
```

That step builds `pnm-cli`, `cnm-cli`, `vta-mcp` and `vta-mobile-core`, which no `-p` flag in the job mentions. A gate derived from those flags would have been **narrower than the job**, and would have skipped that coverage for a change to one of those crates — a filter that silently covers less than it claims, which is the exact failure `ci-affects.sh`'s own docstring is written against.

So the maximal combination moves to **`Feature combos (all-features)`**, gated on the whole workspace (`vta_tests || vtc_tests` — between them, every crate), so it skips only a change touching no crate at all. Bonus: 4 minutes off the critical path, and the two run in parallel.

## The package list is derived, never written down

`scripts/ci-feature-combo-pkgs.sh` reads the scope out of the job's own `-p` flags. A hand-kept "crates Feature combos covers" would be a second description of what the job's steps already say, and the docstring on `ci-affects.sh` records three incidents from exactly that (#1252, #1256, #1259).

It **refuses** if a `--workspace` step ever reappears in the job, naming the line — because that is precisely what makes the `-p` flags an incomplete account. Verified by putting one back:

```
refusing: the Feature combos job has a --workspace step, so the packages
its -p flags name are not the full set it builds. Move that step to the
features-all job, or this filter will under-cover it:
65:        run: cargo check --workspace --features something
```

## What the gate actually does

Probed with real single-file commits against the derived scope:

| change | verdict |
|---|---|
| `docs/02-vta/rate-limiting.md` | skip — only prose and non-build files changed |
| `pnm-cli/src/setup.rs` | skip |
| `cnm-cli/src/main.rs` | skip |
| `vta-mcp/src/guard.rs` | skip |
| `vta-service/src/lib.rs` | **run** |
| `vtc-service/src/backup.rs` | **run** |

Fail-safe in the direction that costs minutes: `.github/`, `scripts/`, `Cargo.lock`, a root manifest, an unattributable path, or any non-PR event all resolve to **run**.

## And a budget it fits in

~40 minutes of work against a 45-minute ceiling made every run a coin flip. An overrun also doesn't present as a failure — GitHub marks the step that was in flight `cancelled`, which reads as though a human cancelled the run, and #1575 spent three attempts getting one verdict out of it. 60 budgets the tail rather than the mean.

## Not in this PR

The job recompiles the dependency graph for each feature set because `target/` is deliberately uncached (#1133: a source-only change doesn't move `Cargo.lock`, so the key doesn't move and stale workspace artifacts get restored).

That objection is right about `actions/cache` and not about `Swatinem/rust-cache`, which evicts workspace-member artifacts before saving and keeps only dependency ones — the same distinction the existing comment draws when it says the registry cache is safe because it is content-addressed. It's already used in `join-didcomm-soak.yml` and pinned by SHA. Worth measuring separately; the open question is its cache size against the repo's 10 GB allowance, given #891 already showed one fat cache evicting the rest.

## Verification

- `shellcheck scripts/ci-feature-combo-pkgs.sh` — clean
- YAML parses; asserted the gate, the 60-minute budget, the new `affects` output, and that the all-features step left one job and landed in the other
- Guard verified to fire, and the derived scope verified against six real commits
